title: 'Cover Story: Banks shift tokenisation into higher gear
body: 'Cover Story: Banks shift tokenisation into higher gear This article first appeared in Wealth, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 Tokenisation, the act of representing an asset or claim as a token on a distributed ledger or blockchain, has remained under the radar among local financial institutions. Until recently. The catalyst, market observers say, came from Bank Negara Malaysia, when it launched the Digital Asset Innovation Hub (DAIH) in June 2025 and published its discussion paper on asset tokenisation in the Malaysian financial sector in October 2025. The public feedback window for the discussion paper closed on March 1, 2026, and Bank Negara hosted its third Asset Tokenisation Industry Working Group session in August this year. The discussion paper states that proof-of-concepts and live pilots will be conducted in a controlled environment through the DAIH this year, with testing expected to continue into 2027, alongside the compilation and publication of findings and the evaluation of key insights. Three banks have launched initiatives under the DAIH. The banks are under CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB); Standard Chartered Bank Malaysia Bhd (Standard Chartered Malaysia), together with Capital A Bhd (KL:CAPITALA); and Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK). Chu Kok Wei, CEO of group wholesale banking and corporate treasurer at CIMB Group, says Malaysian banks are not the earliest to embrace the technology, but they have been moving fast recently. “We might be the country that’s moving at the fastest speed in Southeast Asia in the last one year, based on my observation, by looking at all the stakeholders and our experience and conversation with regulators,” he says. His observation coincides with the findings of HSBC’s Redefining Treasury in Asia Pacific 2026: Voices of Treasury report, published on Sept 17. The report notes that Malaysia stands out as the most enthusiastic market in the region on digital currency adoption, with 50% of respondents saying they were very likely to use digital currencies in the next two years, far higher than the regional average of 19%. Digital currency is tokenised money, which can take the form of tokenised deposits, stablecoins or central bank digital currency. Some 42% of respondents in Malaysia also say digital assets in treasury are high risk, broadly in line with the regional average of 44%, even as they see both opportunity and complexity. The biggest benefits of tokenisation, which is underpinned by blockchain or distributed ledger technology, are greater treasury efficiency (73%) and enhanced liquidity management (50%). “The challenge now is for market infrastructure to catch up to the demand,” says Anand Mukati, head of global payments solutions at HSBC Malaysia. Elsewhere, global banks in developed markets such as the US have been moving fast in tokenisation by adopting blockchain technology. In its Tokenisation 2030: Wall Street On-Chain report published in June, US-based multinational bank Citigroup points out that tokenisation is moving towards operational reality. The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation (DTCC), the US industry-owned clearing house and central securities depository, received regulatory clearance in late 2025 to offer a tokenisation service for DTCC-custodied assets, with a three-year pilot planned for late 2026. The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) announced plans for a tokenised securities platform by late 2026, subject to regulatory approval, which would enable 24/7 trading of US-listed equities and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with near-instant settlement and stablecoin-based funding. Nasdaq has also received the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) approval to enable certain stocks and ETFs to be issued, traded and settled in tokenised form. “These organisations are not crypto-native firms pushing blockchain, but some of the oldest and largest financial institutions adopting new infrastructure,” according to Citi. On Sept 17, the SEC unveiled its long-awaited exemption that will allow companies to offer trading in blockchain-based or “tokenised” stocks and other securities. Four days later, the European Central Bank launched preparatory work to invest a small portion of its own fund in tokenised securities, enabling it to gain practical experience as an investor and build institutional expertise in the use of distributed ledger technology in financial markets. The world is moving fast. Completed and ongoing initiatives When Khazanah Nasional Bhd completed its RM100 million tokenised sukuk pilot project in mid-May, CIMB acted as its sole principal adviser, sole lead arranger and sole facility agent. About three months later, the bank took that experience further, completing the country’s first pilot testing of the settlement of tokenised sukuk using tokenised deposits in a controlled environment. For comparison, Khazanah’s tokenised sukuk pilot project settled the exchange of sukuk on the blockchain, but its cash transactions were conducted through traditional banking channels in fiat currency instead of tokenised deposits. Put simply, a tokenised deposit is a form of digital money that is transferred and settled on a secure blockchain or distributed ledger, rather than through traditional payment infrastructure such as PayNet’s Real-time Retail Payments Platform (RPP) or Bank Negara’s RENTAS+. In an interview with Wealth, CIMB’s Chu says the bank’s pilot project represents a meaningful breakthrough, with CIMB Islamic Bank Bhd issuing RM1.68 billion in sukuk under its existing RM10 billion senior sukuk wakalah programme, across tenors of five, seven, 10 and 15 years. Of the total issuance, RM1.38 billion was represented in tokenised form and subscribed by 12 institutional investors. Both legs of the transaction — CIMB’s tokenised sukuk and the tokenised deposits used to pay for them — were settled on the bank’s own blockchain, CIMB Blockchain Connect. “Khazanah’s tokenised sukuk pilot project was RM100 million with a one-year tenure. We were part of the consortium that arranged the transaction. We took that learning and, in less than five months, we printed our own transaction of RM1.68 billion, out of which RM1.38 billion was tokenised up to 15 years. “This progression is important. That means we are moving from a pilot size transaction to a market size transaction backed by real investor demand,” he says. Institutions that subscribed to CIMB’s tokenised sukuk include sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, insurers, corporates and asset managers, reflecting market confidence in the programme. “We like to think that we have built enough momentum for this to carry forward,” says Chu. The DAIH’s official website lists the initiatives of the three banks. CIMB focuses on tokenised deposits for the settlement of tokenised securities, Maybank on tokenised deposits for payments, and Standard Chartered Malaysia and Capital A on ringgit stablecoins for business-to-business (B2B) settlement. Maybank also played a leading role as joint lead manager, custodian and primary subscriber of Khazanah's RM100 million tokenised sukuk pilot project. In an email response, Maybank global head of markets structuring and quants Rivai Tan says the bank has explored and tested use cases within its own environment to accelerate learning. “This led to initiatives spanning tokenised deposits, near real-time cross-border payments and tokenised investment solution pilots,” he says. Among the initiatives Maybank is involved in is a RM1 million pilot transaction for tokenised supply chain financing, announced on Aug 20 and aimed at enhancing transparency and resilience across supply chain ecosystems. The transaction was carried out in partnership with Virtual Economy Technology Sdn Bhd (V System) via its tokenisation platform, NexA. V System is a participant in the Securities Commission Malaysia’s regulatory sandbox to pilot innovative blockchain-based solutions. Earlier, on March 30, the bank successfully completed the first transaction of its tokenised deposits and cross-border payments with energy infrastructure company Yinson Holdings Bhd (KL:YINSON). The project integrates the tokenisation of bank deposits with an on-chain foreign exchange (FX) conversion of ringgit to Singapore dollars, and a subsequent cross-border payment between the two countries in near real-time, using Maybank’s permissioned blockchain. “Our focus is on turning tokenisation from concept into real-world applications,” says Tan. Maybank Singapore has also joined the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s BLOOM initiative, an industry project to improve cross-border payments using tokenised bank liabilities and regulated stablecoins through an interoperable digital financial system. On the ringgit stablecoin initiative for B2B settlement with Capital A, Standard Chartered Malaysia interim CEO, head of coverage and chief financial officer Mushahid Syed says: “It is still in an initial testing phase. We will share further details subject to approval from Bank Negara.” In his email response, Mushahid Syed adds that the bank’s focus is on connecting tokenised assets to the wider ecosystem, including digital money, custody, trading, collateral and settlement infrastructure. “This includes exploring how digital forms of money can interact more seamlessly with tokenised assets, enabling more efficient access to yield-bearing investment products, and how these tokenised assets themselves can be used as collateral across the financial ecosystem,” he says. Trading tokenised bonds and sukuk on the blockchain While not spelling out the bank’s next step on its tokenisation initiative, CIMB’s Chu says market players would expect the trading of CIMB’s tokenised sukuk on the blockchain. “We started with the issuance of tokenised securities. Bonds and sukuk being a tradable instrument, naturally, industry players would look at how we can trade these tokenised securities more efficiently [on the blockchain] and start to harness the benefits of it,” he says. Halogen Capital, the country’s first digital asset manager, is one of the institutions that subscribed to CIMB’s tokenised sukuk. Its founder and CEO Hann Liew echoes Chu’s view. “We purchased one lot of CIMB tokenised sukuk, and CIMB gives us access to view the tokens. There’s an online platform where institutional investors like us can log in and see our holdings. Put simply, it is like CIMB Octo for retail users, where you can log in and see your details. “However, the challenge is the next step, which is to enable active on-chain trading of the sukuk, which isn’t yet live. Can we see transactions that happened on the blockchain? Can we conduct analysis and trade on it?” he says. One might ask how it is different when tokenised sukuk is traded on the blockchain. Chu points to several key features, including instant settlement, round-the-clock trading and fractionalisation. With a distributed ledger shared across various parties, a trade executed on the blockchain can be settled almost instantaneously — otherwise known as “atomic settlement” — which reduces settlement risk. Settlement risk is the danger that the money is paid but the securities are not delivered, or vice versa. A classic example dates back to 1974, when banks globally paid Deutsche marks to German lender Herstatt Bank in the morning but did not receive the US dollars they expected later in the day. Herstatt had made wrong directional bets on the greenback and was shut down by regulators midday, with the value of transactions left unsettled estimated at US$200 million. Settlement risk becomes severe when large sums are involved. Meanwhile, when trades can be matched, settled and recorded automatically and efficiently, bonds and sukuk can be traded round the clock, translating into cost savings and a potentially more vibrant market. Tokenised securities and deposits are programmable, which is where smart contracts come into play. A smart contract is code on a blockchain that automatically carries out the terms of an agreement when conditions are met, without human intervention. Chu says smart contracts can be used for market events. For instance, where a bond or sukuk pays a coupon every six months, the profit can be distributed automatically via the distributed ledger. “All these are baby steps that we are taking, from the primary market to secondary, and eventually it covers even redemptions,” he says. Tokenised securities can be fractionalised, which opens up the possibility of tokenised bonds and sukuk becoming easily accessible to retail investors at a much lower amount. But Chu says tokenisation and blockchain are merely a technological enabler; further democratisation of bonds and sukuk would require changes in rules and regulations. “We all need to kind of contain our excitement about how tokenisation enables retail participation for now. It provides a platform, but suitability for investors, fair disclosure [of information] and all other relevant processes have to be continuously assessed by the regulators,” he says. Interoperability between blockchains, and between the new and old systems Against such a backdrop, tokenisation initiatives undertaken by local banks are based on the “digital twin” concept, which means the on-chain token mirrors the traditional legal records rather than replacing them. “From a legal sense, digital twin means the whole process of the issuance of CIMB sukuk follows existing rules and regulations and contract. The original contract remains valid, while the digital token is only a replica. In this case, you don’t need to answer what is the relationship of the replica and the underlying assets,” says Chu. However, the country’s rules and regulations will need to change if financial services were to move fully onto the blockchain, which is one of the challenges in tokenisation. Chu says other challenges include interoperability, which means the deployment of digital tokens across the different blockchains of different banks. However, he says CIMB prefers to focus on something else: the interoperability between the new technology, which is the blockchain, and the existing ones, especially in the bond market. “This is much more important as bonds and sukuk are an established asset class with a total value of more than RM2 trillion in the system. How can these assets slowly evolve over time, so that people can embrace the new ones [issued with the new technology] without feeling that the old ones are out of fashion? “This is extremely important, as institutional fund managers can be holding a 30-year bond today. There are many 30-year bonds out there and they start to worry about what happens if all these are going to be tokenised,” he says. Maybank’s Tan agrees that beyond technology and process design, the successful deployment of tokenisation also depends on many other factors, including interoperability, regulatory alignment and broader industry adoption. From a practical perspective, a key challenge lies in integrating tokenised solutions into existing systems, processes and operating models, he adds. This means a bank needs to stay forward-looking and rethink workflows from the ground up, including what should be retained, rebuilt, simplified or, in some cases, fundamentally redesigned to realise the full benefits of tokenisation. “Realising the full potential of tokenisation will require close collaboration among regulators, financial institutions and technology providers to establish common standards and trusted market infrastructure,” says Tan. Standard Chartered Malaysia’s Mushahid Syed adds that developing digital infrastructure that offers accessible, cost-effective and instant alternative wholesale payments is key for a trading nation like Malaysia, with its strong small and medium enterprise base. There is little doubt that tokenisation, underpinned by blockchain technology, will make banking and financial services more efficient and effective when it matures. Workflows, organisational structures and the content of certain jobs may evolve. Changes are already afoot. “An example I always tell everyone is that we are now using iPhone 18, which has evolved significantly from its first version. The same applies to the evolution of the financial services industry and the role of people working in it,” says Chu. Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: 'Era of Cheap Debt Is Over as Corporates Face Tightening Credits — BIMB Securities
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 28): The era of cheap debt is over and rising global bond yields will squeeze earnings, pushing some corporates towards bank loans, BIMB Securities said. Credit conditions are tightening, hurting firms with unhedged floating rate debts, large refinancing needs and those facing upcoming maturities, the research house said. Capital-intensive and highly leveraged companies face greater earnings risk, amplified by weaker credit quality, the house noted. “In contrast, we see tech as one of the outlier sectors — where most stocks are actually net cash,” BIMB Securities said in a note. Unlike true artificial intelligence firms or data centre operators grappling with intensive capital expenditure plans, Malaysian tech stocks is a key rotation sector for the coming era of elevated rates, the house noted. The US Federal Reserve raised interest rate earlier this month for the first time in three years, sending the yield on the 10-year benchmark Malaysian Government Securities to as high as 4.18% before moderating. Bond issuances hit record highs in 2025 and corporates have continued to sell more debt this year tapping into the relatively inexpensive markets. “But this is likely to change as global rates outlook shifts to higher for longer,” BIMB Securities said. The house’s view is for the yield on 10-year government bonds to hold around 3.90% till end of the year but shift towards 4.00% by end-2027. Among the top 100 firms by market capitalisation, utilities, property, telecommunications, construction, healthcare and real estate investment trusts are the most exposed sectors, BIMB Securities flagged. The house also singled out IOI Properties Group Bhd (KL:IOIPG) for its high floating rate debt exposure. Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) and Genting Malaysia Bhd (KL:GENM) were also highlighted as both companies will have to come to the market to refinance substantial debt with sizeable maturities over the next 12 months. Banking stocks, meanwhile, could benefit from the shift, especially those with strong corporate lending franchises, the research house said. Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK), CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB) and RHB Bank Bhd (KL:RHBBANK), in particular, could benefit from the temporary migration of borrowers from the bond market to bank loans, the house said. full_text: 'Era of Cheap Debt Is Over as Corporates Face Tightening Credits — BIMB Securities. 'KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 28): The era of cheap debt is over and rising global bond yields will squeeze earnings, pushing some corporates towards bank loans, BIMB Securities said. Credit conditions are tightening, hurting firms with unhedged floating rate debts, large refinancing needs and those facing upcoming maturities, the research house said. Capital-intensive and highly leveraged companies face greater earnings risk, amplified by weaker credit quality, the house noted. “In contrast, we see tech as one of the outlier sectors — where most stocks are actually net cash,” BIMB Securities said in a note. Unlike true artificial intelligence firms or data centre operators grappling with intensive capital expenditure plans, Malaysian tech stocks is a key rotation sector for the coming era of elevated rates, the house noted. The US Federal Reserve raised interest rate earlier this month for the first time in three years, sending the yield on the 10-year benchmark Malaysian Government Securities to as high as 4.18% before moderating. Bond issuances hit record highs in 2025 and corporates have continued to sell more debt this year tapping into the relatively inexpensive markets. “But this is likely to change as global rates outlook shifts to higher for longer,” BIMB Securities said. The house’s view is for the yield on 10-year government bonds to hold around 3.90% till end of the year but shift towards 4.00% by end-2027. Among the top 100 firms by market capitalisation, utilities, property, telecommunications, construction, healthcare and real estate investment trusts are the most exposed sectors, BIMB Securities flagged. The house also singled out IOI Properties Group Bhd (KL:IOIPG) for its high floating rate debt exposure. Genting Bhd (KL:GENTING) and Genting Malaysia Bhd (KL:GENM) were also highlighted as both companies will have to come to the market to refinance substantial debt with sizeable maturities over the next 12 months. Banking stocks, meanwhile, could benefit from the shift, especially those with strong corporate lending franchises, the research house said. Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK), CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB) and RHB Bank Bhd (KL:RHBBANK), in particular, could benefit from the temporary migration of borrowers from the bond market to bank loans, the house said. title: 'Maybank completes acquisition of remaining interest in Maybank Ageas
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank) has completed the proposed acquisition of the remaining 30.95 per cent interest in Maybank Ageas Holdings Bhd after signing a share purchase agreement with Ageas Insurance International NV (Ageas) on Sept 8, 2026. In a statement today, the bank said it completed the acquisition after receiving regulatory approval from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) on Sept 1, 2026. Maybank Ageas is the holding company for the Etiqa business in Malaysia and Singapore, providing a full range of life and general conventional insurance products as well as family and general takaful products through multi-channel distribution. Maybank president and group chief executive officer Datuk Seri Khairussaleh Ramli said the acquisition's completion was a major milestone for the bank as it continues to advance Etiqa's ambition to be a national champion, expand across Southeast Asia and build a global takaful powerhouse under ROAR30. "With Maybank Ageas being a wholly owned subsidiary of Maybank, it strengthens Etiqa's position as a national insurance and takaful champion, driving deeper penetration of Maybank's customer base. "Our focus will be unlocking further value for our customers across Southeast Asia via our regional wealth propositions through cross-selling and delivering more integrated and personalised financial solutions," he added. Meanwhile, the bank said Maybank Ageas is expected to remain well-positioned to capture growth opportunities in the insurance and takaful sector, supported by Maybank's extensive customer base and distribution network, and the increasing market demand for more integrated and personalised protection solutions.

title: 'Felda’s road ahead in the spotlight
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Seven years after Malaysians were made aware of the problems confronting the Federal Land Development Authority (Felda), the institution is once again at a crossroads. Felda, which has the largest plantation footprint in the country and has helped improve the livelihoods of more than 100,000 original settlers and their families, is undergoing another strategic review amid concerns over its long-term sustainability. An interim report on the Felda Group Strategic Roadmap 2025-2030 (HTF 30) was submitted last month by the Special Committee on the Strategic Plan for Felda Group to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim. Among the proposals under consideration is a redefinition of Felda’s mandate, including a review of the Land Development Act that governs the agency, as the committee monitors actions taken following the 2019 Felda White Paper, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The review comes as the highly indebted entity grapples with crucial replanting costs that could reach RM900 million annually, on top of more than RM900 million in financing costs currently borne by the government. Felda oversees some 870,000 hectares (ha) of land, of which 490,000ha was allocated to settlers, 330,000ha to Felda’s commercial plantations — later placed under FGV Holdings Bhd — and another 50,000ha for village development. Fragmented and ineffective management of the land and operations, together with questionable transactions and investments, resulted in heavy losses despite Felda receiving billions of ringgit from the listing of its commercial arm, then known as Felda Global Ventures Holdings Bhd. By 2017, Felda’s borrowings had ballooned to RM12.1 billion from just RM100 million in 2007. In 2023, the government guaranteed and agreed to service Felda’s RM9.9 billion sukuk, issued to fund the RM3.7 billion privatisation of FGV to consolidate its estate operations, as well as Felda and settlers’ debt. But more needs to be done before those efforts bear fruit. Huge capital needed to become sustainable In 2012, Felda raised RM6 billion through the offer for sale of FGV shares during the latter’s initial public offering, while FGV itself raised RM4.5 billion from investors. In total, the exercise raised RM10.5 billion. Instead of directing more of those proceeds towards critical needs such as replanting, the 2019 Felda White Paper found that RM4.6 billion, or 76% of Felda’s IPO proceeds, went towards what it described as “unproductive spending”, while another RM1.4 billion was channelled into investments that failed to generate returns. The spending included RM1.69 billion in special payments to settlers, RM550 million in one-off contributions to state governments, RM400 million in loans for settlers’ house extensions, RM406 million to redeem FGV shares and RM177 million in listing expenses. FGV, meanwhile, spent RM3.3 billion, or 73% of its RM4.5 billion in IPO proceeds, on investments and developments that did not generate satisfactory returns. FGV, which leased Felda’s plantation land, also failed to achieve the yields Felda had projected, leaving the agency with an earnings shortfall. Following FGV’s privatisation, Felda is looking at consolidating the management of its commercial estates and settlers’ land. But that alone will not resolve the underlying balance-sheet problem, particularly the heavy capital requirements needed to keep the estates productive. The role of Felda Beyond its plantation operations, Felda bears significant social obligations to settlers, including spending on housing, infrastructure and income support for up to five years during the replanting cycle. Today, the families of Felda settlers span as many as six generations and number about 2.8 million people. In many respects, Felda has fulfilled its original mandate of opening up rural land and developing communities alongside settlers, about 95% of whom have received titles to their land. Without a clear framework for its future model, the institution’s role and the financial obligations that come with it risk continuing to be shaped by factors beyond its core mandate, particularly when political considerations intersect with policy during periods of adjustment. Any new roadmap will therefore have to define more clearly where Felda’s commercial responsibilities end and its social obligations begin, and how each should be funded. Felda’s troubled investments Felda was in better shape before the mismanagement that followed the windfall from FGV’s listing, when the institution was earning around RM3 billion a year. There are also arguments that greater provisions should have been made for replanting, which is central to sustaining its core operations. Poor investment decisions, however, turned Felda’s fortunes upside down in less than a decade. A forensic audit found RM2.2 billion in asset impairments from eight transactions undertaken by Felda and Felda Investment Corporation Sdn Bhd (FIC) between 2010 and 2018 — equivalent to half of their initial RM4.4 billion investment value. Among them were PT Eagle High Plantations Tbk, the Kuala Lumpur Vertical City (KLVC) project, and several London properties. One of the largest was Felda’s US$505.4 million acquisition of a 37% non-controlling stake in Eagle High Plantations in 2016 at a premium, resulting in an impairment loss of RM1.576 billion in 2017. Its London property purchases also came under scrutiny over discrepancies between reported acquisition prices and amounts received by vendors, while some properties saw their values fall sharply soon after acquisition. KLVC, meanwhile, remains the subject of a legal dispute between Felda and developer Synergy Promenade Sdn Bhd (SPSB) over the development of Felda land along Jalan Semarak. Former FIC chief executive officer Mohd Zaid Abdul Jalil has also been charged with two counts of cheating the company’s board, which allegedly resulted in the ownership of 16 land parcels being transferred from Felda to SPSB.

title: 'Behind the remittances: The social cost of the OFW economy
body: 'The overseas Filipino worker phenomenon reflects a structural economic failure that began 50 years ago, when what was intended as a temporary response to unemployment and economic pressure evolved into a permanent development strategy.  To understand why the Philippines now has an entire Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), created in 2021, along with agencies and systems such as the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA), Philippine Overseas Employment Administration (POEA), overseas employment certificates (OECs) and Philippine Overseas Labor Offices (POLOs), it is necessary to look back at how labor migration became embedded in the economy.  From a few thousand to 10 million  Before 1972, overseas employment was marginal, with fewer than 3,000 Filipinos leaving for work each year. They were mostly seafarers, U.S. Navy stewards and professionals who went to the United States after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965.  The Philippines was still a net importer of labor, with Americans and Chinese managing factories.  In 1974, President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. issued the Labor Code of the Philippines, or Presidential Decree No. 442, and created the Overseas Employment Development Board and the National Seamen Board.  The move came amid two major pressures: the 1973 oil shock and unemployment at home.  Oil-producing countries in the Middle East suddenly had enormous revenues and needed foreign workers for large construction projects, particularly in Saudi Arabia, Libya and the United Arab Emirates.  The United States, under Henry Kissinger, encouraged labor-exporting allies to send workers to the region, helping absorb petrodollars while supporting continued oil flows.  At home, official unemployment was 7% to 8%, while underemployment was above 20%. Martial law had also coincided with the closure of small factories that could not compete after import liberalization, while unrest continued in the countryside.  Exporting surplus labor became a political and economic safety valve.  Marcos initially envisioned the manpower export program as temporary, lasting two or three years during the Middle East construction boom before workers returned home.  In 1975, the Philippines deployed 36,035 workers. By 1980, the number had reached about 200,000 a year.  By 1983, during the debt crisis, overseas employment had become part of government economic policy, with remittances providing dollars that could help service the country’s foreign debt.  After the 1986 Edsa People Power Revolution, succeeding administrations retained and expanded the system.  President Corazon Aquino institutionalized the POEA in 1987 and referred to OFWs as “Bagong Bayani.” President Fidel Ramos developed the OWWA fund and promoted Filipino workers as “world class” in 1994. The Estrada and Arroyo administrations later incorporated deployment targets into economic planning.  By 2006, annual deployments had reached 1 million.  By 2024, the Philippine Statistics Authority counted 10.1 million overseas Filipinos — 6.1 million temporary workers or OFWs and 4 million permanent immigrants — along with 1.8 million irregular migrants.  That year, overseas Filipinos remitted $38.34 billion, equivalent to 8.9% of gross domestic product directly. When the multiplier effect on consumption is included, the report estimates that remittances account for almost 20% of the economy.  Without those remittances, the report argues, the peso could have fallen to P80 to the dollar and the country could have faced a debt crisis similar to Sri Lanka’s.  What began with a few thousand workers grew into a diaspora of millions over five decades.  The costs behind the remittances  The country closely tracks the dollars OFWs send home, but the social costs are less visible.  Family disintegration  Fifty-eight percent of OFW households are headed by women left behind or by grandparents.  Studies by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies and UNICEF cited in the report show that children of OFWs have a 40% higher incidence of anxiety, low school performance and teenage pregnancy.  Long-distance parenting through video calls cannot fully replace a parent’s physical presence.  Many marriages also break down. Annulment cases in Cebu and Pampanga courts cited in the report identify having an OFW spouse as the second most common ground after infidelity.  The result has been a generation of children raised partly through mobile phones and other forms of remote communication.  Lost motherhood and fatherhood  The Philippines exports about 180,000 domestic helpers and caregivers each year to places including Hong Kong, Singapore, Saudi Arabia and Italy.  Their departure creates another question at home: Who cares for their own children and elderly relatives?  Often, that work falls to another woman from a poorer community who may also be separated from her own child.  The report describes this as a chain of care deficits and says the Philippines now has 1.2 million abandoned elderly people in rural areas.  Trafficking, abuse and death  Since 2010, the DMW has recorded about 24,000 OFWs in distress, in jail or experiencing abuse every year, according to the report.  Among the most prominent cases are Mary Jane Veloso, Flor Contemplacion, who was executed in Singapore in 1995, and Joanna Demafelis, whose body was found in a freezer in Kuwait in 2018.  Every year, 400 to 500 OFWs return home in coffins, the report says.  Contract substitution, denial of days off, rape and unpaid wages remain recurring problems, particularly for poor women deployed to countries with weak labor protections.  The Philippine government also faces limits in protecting workers while maintaining diplomatic and labor relations with host countries.  Brain drain and deskilling  The report estimates that training a nurse in publicly supported institutions such as the University of the Philippines and Philippine General Hospital costs about P1.2 million.  After training, some nurses leave to work overseas, including in the United States, where they earn far more and pay taxes to their host country.  For three decades, the Philippines exported about 19,000 nurses a year even as the domestic nurse-to-patient ratio stood at 1:45, compared with the World Health Organization standard of 1:12 cited in the report.  During the COVID-19 pandemic, the country faced a shortage of intensive care nurses while many Filipino nurses were working abroad.  Similar patterns affect teachers, engineers, seafarers and information technology workers.  Deskilling creates another problem. Teachers may become domestic workers in Dubai, while agriculturists may work as cleaners in Qatar. Over time, professional skills may deteriorate, and many workers never return to the fields for which they were trained.  A consumption-driven economy  Remittances also have broader economic effects.  Large inflows of foreign currency help keep the peso relatively strong, making exports more expensive and imports cheaper.  The report argues that this dynamic weakens domestic factories and agriculture because imported goods can become cheaper than locally produced alternatives.  Families often use remittances to buy homes, consumer goods and education rather than to build factories or other productive enterprises.  Consumption rises, but investment in productive capital does not necessarily follow.  The report says the manufacturing share of GDP fell from 38% in 1960 to 18% in 2024, describing it as the lowest in Southeast Asia.  A political cushion  Remittances can also reduce pressure on the government to create jobs at home.  When unemployment can be partly addressed through overseas deployment, governments face less urgency to reform land ownership, strengthen industry or improve domestic employment conditions, according to the report.  Remittances also help families withstand economic hardship, potentially reducing social pressure that might otherwise force more sweeping reforms.  In this sense, OFW income has served not only as a household lifeline but also as a broader political and economic cushion.  A culture of leaving  After five decades of large-scale migration, working abroad has become deeply embedded in Filipino ideas of success.  For many young people, aspirations increasingly center on careers in Canada, the Middle East or elsewhere rather than on agriculture, manufacturing or other industries at home.  The result is a culture in which leaving the country is often viewed as a primary path to upward mobility.  What if more workers had stayed?  One of the central questions raised by the OFW experience is what might have happened had millions of the country’s most ambitious, English-speaking and mobile workers remained in the Philippines.  According to the Commission on Higher Education, the country produces about 750,000 college graduates each year.  The report estimates that roughly 30% plan to leave within five years, or about 225,000 graduates annually.  It argues that retaining more of those workers could have significantly increased the country’s stock of skilled human capital.  But the effect would not have been limited to numbers.  A nurse who remains in the country may demand a better health system, open a clinic or press the government to build hospitals. An engineer may open a machine shop or contribute to local industry.  South Korea offers a comparison cited in the report.  In 1965, South Korea sent about 50,000 workers to West Germany as miners and nurses. But the government of Park Chung-hee used remittances while developing industries such as POSCO steel and Hyundai shipbuilding and encouraged workers to return with skills.  The Philippines, by contrast, continued to expand overseas deployment.  Had more Filipino workers stayed, the report argues that three major changes might have followed. The remaining workers must seek employment abroad, accept lower-quality jobs or remain unemployed.  The report also argues that remittances can reinforce this cycle by giving households additional resources while reducing pressure to improve agricultural productivity. Bangladesh, meanwhile, reduced the share of overseas-worker income in its economy from 8% to 3% of GDP after expanding its garment industry. title: 'Berjaya Says Core Berjaya Hills Businesses Unaffected by Pahang Enforcement Action
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Berjaya Corp Bhd (KL:BJCORP) said its main businesses at Berjaya Hills remain fully operational despite enforcement action by the Pahang authorities, and expects no material financial or operational impact from the issue. It said state authorities had sealed and restricted access to the staff quarters, central laundry, rabbit park and Japanese garden on Sept 28, while The Chateau Spa & Wellness Resort, Colmar Tropicale Hotel, Berjaya Hills Golf & Country Club and the greenhouses were unaffected. "The group's core operating facilities, including the hotels, golf club and greenhouses remain unaffected and continue to operate as usual," Berjaya Corp said in a bourse filing Tuesday. The disclosure was made in response to Bursa Malaysia's queries seeking details of the enforcement action — linked to a long-running dispute between Berjaya Hills Resort Bhd and the Pahang government over a sharp increase in quit rent imposed on the company's properties in the state — and how it would financially and operationally affect the group. Berjaya Hills claimed its annual quit rent jumped 13-fold to RM33.7 million in 2020 from about RM2.4 million in 2019, before being reduced to RM25.75 million following 11 appeals to the state government between April 2020 and December 2022. The company said it paid about RM42.65 million in quit rent and penalties "under protest" between 2020 and 2026, while continuing to seek a further review of the rates. In Tuesday's filing, Berjaya Corp said the higher quit rent expenses had been recognised through accruals for the respective financial years since the revised rates took effect in 2020. "Accordingly, the impact arising from the revised annual quit rent rates has been taken into account in the group's financial statements for the respective financial years and the revised rates have no material operational impact to the group," it added. Separately on Tuesday, Pahang Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Wan Rosdy Wan Ismail said the state government is open to discussions with Berjaya Hills to resolve the impasse, but stressed that any talks must be guided by existing legal provisions and regulations. "That is up to them (Berjaya Hills). We are taking actions based on the law. The state government is open to discussions, but they must be based on and guided by the law. There are regulations, so follow the rules," Wan Rosdy was quoted as saying by Bernama. Berjaya Hills had on Oct 2 called the enforcement action "unconscionable and totally unacceptable", arguing that it was unreasonable given that its application for leave to appeal the quit rent dispute remains pending before the Federal Court. Nevertheless, it also said it hoped the Pahang government would continue to engage with the company towards a "mutually acceptable and amicable resolution". The company, which has been challenging the revised quit rent through legal means with no success so far, first sought a judicial review at the Temerloh High Court. The application was dismissed in May 2024 on grounds that the court could not intervene in the state government's policy decision. That decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal on July 16 this year. This led to Berjaya Hills applying for leave to appeal to the Federal Court on Aug 14, with the hearing scheduled for Dec 8. Berjaya Corp closed unchanged at 25 sen on Tuesday for a market capitalisation of RM1.52 billion. body: 'It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge ’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception.  “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.”  The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd.  Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation.  Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore. Giggs cautioned that strong domestic academy pipelines must anchor sustainable progress in football. Speaking to reporters in the capital, the 13-time Premier League winner addressed the accelerating trend across the region, where nations including Malaysia and Indonesia have increasingly turned to foreign-born and heritage players to fast-track competitiveness on the continental stage. Giggs, himself a celebrated graduate of United's famed "Class of '92" youth system, offered his take on the debate and said that while outside talent can raise immediate standards, it should never come at the expense of grassroots development. "I think everything is always a balance," Giggs said when asked if relying on naturalised players is a sound strategy for lower-ranked nations looking to climb the ladder. "Where it's countries or leagues outside the big leagues, you need the infrastructure of academy players coming through. "And also, the foreign players coming in, they need to be good quality, good professionals." The 53-year-old former Wales manager also pointed out the critical role of coaching in bridging the developmental gap, noting that importing tactical expertise must serve to elevate local coaching standards rather than displace them. "The coaching, if possible, I think should be local," he said. "But obviously, if you bring in experienced coaches from other countries, they can also help show the professionalism and introduce different tactical ideas. "It's always a balance. But I think for any country, it's always good if you have your own players coming through from an early age, though of course, they have to be good enough." title: 'MKH bakal dinyahsenarai selepas Batu Kawan kuasai 95.16% saham | DagangNews - Berita Bisnes Anda
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR 1 Okt – MKH Bhd bakal dinyahsenarai daripada Bursa Malaysia selepas Batu Kawan Bhd bersama anak syarikatnya, Whitmore Holdings Sdn Bhd serta pihak yang bertindak bersama mereka menguasai 95.16% saham syarikat pemaju hartanah itu. Jumlah pegangan tersebut bersamaan 548.85 juta saham MKH setakat penutupan dagangan pada 30 Sept 2026, menurut kenyataan yang dikeluarkan oleh Maybank Investment Bank Bhd bagi pihak Batu Kawan dan Whitmore. Dengan pegangan yang sudah melepasi 90%, Batu Kawan dan Whitmore kini boleh mengambil alih baki saham MKH yang masih dipegang pemegang saham yang tidak menerima tawaran pengambilalihan tersebut. Baki saham MKH akan diambil alih secara wajib Langkah itu akan dibuat di bawah Seksyen 222(1) Akta Pasaran Modal dan Perkhidmatan 2007 yang membolehkan baki saham diperoleh secara wajib. Tawaran pengambilalihan pada harga RM2 sesaham itu masih dibuka sehingga 8 Oktober 2026 selepas tarikh tutup asal pada 17 September lalu dilanjutkan. Selepas tempoh tawaran tamat, Bursa Malaysia Securities akan menggantung dagangan saham MKH selepas lima hari pasaran, sebelum Batu Kawan dan Whitmore meneruskan proses untuk menarik balik status penyenaraian MKH. Pengambilalihan MKH bernilai RM1.15 bilion Langkah Batu Kawan mengambil alih MKH bermula pada Mei lalu apabila Whitmore bersetuju membeli kepentingan 47.7% dalam MKH daripada anggota keluarga Chen pada harga RM2 sesaham, membabitkan nilai RM549.8 juta. Pembelian itu kemudiannya disusuli tawaran kepada pemegang saham MKH yang lain pada harga sama bagi membolehkan Batu Kawan meningkatkan pegangannya dalam syarikat tersebut. Secara keseluruhan, pengambilalihan MKH untuk menjadikannya syarikat persendirian bernilai sehingga RM1.15 bilion, termasuk kos pembelian kepentingan awal daripada keluarga Chen. Tawaran RM2 sesaham terima pandangan berbeza Bagaimanapun, tawaran tersebut sebelum ini mendapat pandangan berbeza daripada penasihat bebas MKH dan MKH Oil Palm (East Kalimantan) Bhd, iaitu cabang perladangan MKH yang disenaraikan secara berasingan. Kenanga Investment Bank Bhd, yang bertindak sebagai penasihat bebas MKH, menilai tawaran RM2 sesaham itu sebagai “tidak adil tetapi munasabah”, dengan mengambil kira harga tawaran yang lebih rendah daripada nilai aset wajar MKH. Bagi MKH Oil Palm pula, Mainstreet Advisers Sdn Bhd menggesa pemegang saham menolak tawaran 66.26 sen sesaham daripada Batu Kawan, yang disifatkannya sebagai “tidak adil dan tidak munasabah”. Menurut Mainstreet, harga tawaran itu mewakili diskaun 47% kepada nilai aset bersih (NAV) MKH Oil Palm. Pada masa sama, Batu Kawan bercadang mengekalkan MKH Oil Palm sebagai syarikat yang disenaraikan di Bursa Malaysia.- DagangNews.com

title: 'High Court to rule Oct 23 on Maritime Network’s bid to keep RHB accounts open
body:
'

KUALA LUMPUR: The High Court yesterday fixed Oct 23 to rule on a shipping company’s bid to restrain RHB Bank Berhad from closing two of its long-standing accounts, pending the disposal of its full suit.

Judicial Commissioner Elesabet Paya Wan set the date after hearing submissions from P. Taneswaran, acting for Maritime Network Sdn Bhd, and the bank’s counsel, Gan Khong Aik.

Taneswaran submitted that the bank had failed to establish any breach of terms or requirements by the plaintiff, Maritime Network, that would justify closing its accounts.

He further argued that the bank owed Maritime Network both a fiduciary duty and a duty of care.

Gan countered that no fiduciary relationship or duty of care arose between the bank and the shipping company, submitting that the relationship between a bank and its customer was that of debtor and creditor.

In October last year, the High Court granted a temporary injunction restraining RHB from closing the two long-standing accounts, pending the hearing of the company’s application for a full injunction.

According to court documents, the company has held a multi-currency account and a current account with RHB since 2005.

On Oct 6, 2025, it received a termination notice dated Oct 1, 2025, stating that the bank intended to close both accounts and terminate all related services within 14 days, citing breaches of its internal policies and guidelines.

The company, however, claimed that RHB had failed to specify which policies or guidelines had allegedly been breached.

The plaintiff said an ongoing dispute over the accounts had earlier led to its pre-trial discovery application being dismissed by the High Court on July 2, 2025.

The company subsequently appealed to the Court of Appeal, which in December last year allowed its appeal against the dismissal of the pre-trial discovery application.

The appellate court then ordered RHB to produce its Minimum Due Diligence guidelines governing foreign exchange transactions to the company within 45 days.

Maritime Network further alleged that the bank’s vague allegations placed it in a position of uncertainty, depriving it of any opportunity to defend itself.

The company asserted that this conduct amounted to an abuse of power that prejudiced its rights.

It also claimed that the bank’s conduct demonstrated an intention to oppress rather than protect its legitimate banking interests.

title: 'Scheduling boo-boo: Malaysian hockey league matches originally set for Deepavali rescheduled - Twentytwo13
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: Coaches of Premier League hockey teams scheduled to play on Deepavali day are happy they will now battle it out on different dates, as the Malaysian Hockey Confederation (MHC) repeats its 2018 scheduling boo-boo. Two matches – Terengganu Hockey Team against Armed Forces Hockey Team and TNB Thunderbolts versus Maybank – were originally scheduled for Nov 8, the day Deepavali is celebrated in Malaysia. However, the matches will now be rescheduled, much to the delight of TNB Thunderbolts and Terengganu Hockey Team. Mohd Harfizi Baharom of Terengganu said he had been informed that the match against the soldiers would now be played on Nov 9. “It is good that we will not be playing on such an auspicious day. It gives those celebrating the festival time to spend with their families,” Mohd Harfizi told Twentytwo13. “Several of our players have only just returned from the Asian Games. Unfortunately, there is a packed international calendar and the national team will be off to the Asian Champions Trophy from Oct 27 to Nov 5. “As such, having an extra day to prepare for the match against the Armed Forces is welcome. We are third in the standings, but have not given up hope of winning the title. One day can make a difference.” However, the new dates are not reflected on MHC’s website as of publication time. TNB Thunderbolts coach Nor Saiful Zaini, who is also the national junior coach, said he has yet to receive official notice of the new date. “I know it is not easy for MHC to juggle the calendar, but we shouldn’t play on Deepavali or any other religious festival. I am waiting for confirmation regarding the change of date,” said Nor Saiful. In 2018, the Razak Cup was initially scheduled from Nov 3-11, with Deepavali falling on Nov 6 that year. After protests from teams, especially Negeri Sembilan, which threatened to pull out of the tournament, MHC eventually brought forward the tournament to Oct 26-Nov 3. The repeat of the episode raised eyebrows, as those in charge of scheduling the league should have been fully aware of the festive seasons in the country. Meanwhile, Nor Saiful said he would have his hands full as the national juniors will compete in the Sultan of Johor Cup (Oct 17-24), followed by the Murugappa Gold Cup (Oct 25-Nov 4) in India. Nor Saiful was instrumental in recently guiding the national team to next year’s Junior World Cup. “I will need to juggle my team selection carefully, as we have to consider the league matches as well as the two major tournaments. “Some of the teams may be reluctant to release their junior players, but on the bright side, I have the chance to test more players in Johor and India,” he added.

title: 'BERNAMA - Malaysia Entering More Supportive Water Investment Cycle  -- CIMB Securities
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 (Bernama) -- Malaysia is entering a more supportive water investment cycle as ageing infrastructure, high water losses and rising industrial and data centre demand, as well as greater climate variability are increasing the urgency to improve water efficiency, reliability, and resilience. In a note today, CIMB Securities said the federal government had approved RM1.7 billion under the 13th Malaysia Plan to replace about 1,800 kilometres of critical pipes from 2026 to 2030, alongside a multi-year National Non-Revenue Water (NRW) Programme. It said sizeable projects including Langat 2 Phase 2, Rasau Phase 2, and the Northern Perak Water Supply Scheme should further strengthen water security and provide a visible pipeline for contractors, pipe manufacturers and ancillary solution providers. CIMB Securities said Malaysia’s NRW rate stood at 37.1 per cent in 2024. “Persistently high NRW, ageing distribution networks, and rising climate variability result in unnecessary raw water extraction, higher treatment and pumping requirements, weaker utility economics, and supply disruption risks. “Concurrently, population growth, industrialisation, and rapid data centre development are driving structural water demand, particularly across economic corridors in Selangor, Johor, and Penang,” it added. The stockbroking company said Malaysia’s water transition is seen broadening from purely building new infrastructure towards using existing water resources and assets more efficiently. It said sustainable NRW reduction requires physical rehabilitation alongside smart metering, leak detection, pressure management, telemetry, analytics, and intelligent asset-management systems. “These technologies can make water networks more visible, measurable, and manageable, improving the effectiveness of every ringgit spent on water infrastructure. “This is aligned with the Water Sector Transformation 2040 (WST2040), which promotes digitalisation, climate resilience, integrated water-resource management, and stronger sector governance,” it said. From an investment perspective, CIMB Securities said it favours companies positioned at either the efficiency or infrastructure-enablement layers of Malaysia’s water transition. “Insight Analytics Bhd is among the most direct listed proxies to water digitalisation and NRW management, while Gamuda Bhd offers exposure to large-scale treatment, transmission, and water security projects. “The key near-term risk remains the pace at which funding and policy commitments translate into tenders, project awards, and, ultimately, earnings,” it said. -- BERNAMA BERNAMA provides up-to-date authentic and comprehensive news and information which are disseminated via BERNAMA Wires; www.bernama.com; BERNAMA TV on Astro 502, unifi TV 631 and MYTV 121 channels and BERNAMA Radio on FM93.9 (Klang Valley), FM107.5 (Johor Bahru), FM107.9 (Kota Kinabalu) and FM100.9 (Kuching) frequencies. title: 'Food Waste Forms Nearly 40% of Nation’s Daily Solid Waste, Says Minister
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): Nearly 40% of the total 40,000 metric tonnes of solid waste generated in the country daily consists of food waste, according to Housing and Local Government Minister Nga Kor Ming. He said efforts to address this waste issue require the cooperation of all parties through a "whole-of-nation approach" involving both businesses and consumers to collectively change their attitudes and practices. “This is a form of waste. Food waste is not a crime, but it is a sin. It is a grave sin when edible food is simply thrown away,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat Monday. Nga said this when replying a question from Datuk Mumtaz Md Nawi (PN-Tumpat) regarding the latest developments in efforts to reduce waste sent to landfills and to increase recycling rates. Meanwhile, he expressed confidence that the ministry would achieve its target of exceeding a 40% recycling rate by the end of this year. Nga noted that under the "Trash to Cash" recycling programme, the total collection of recyclable materials between January and August exceeded 7.86 million kilogrammes (kg), with a sales value of over RM2.85 million. “Secondly, the zero-waste community initiative involving the establishment of 17 active zero-waste community centres during the same period has collected over 111,504kg of recyclable materials,” he said. Additionally, Nga said a school-based recycling competition, involving 1,680 schools, successfully collected 4.95 million kilogrammes of recyclable materials, which were sold for RM2.98 million. “Based on calculations of the total collected from 2018 to last year, we managed to gather nearly 20 million kilogrammes of recyclable items, generating proceeds exceeding RM10.22 million,” he said. Responding to a supplementary question from Mumtaz regarding the specific controls and enforcement actions implemented by the Ministry of Housing and Local Government concerning cable theft including penalties imposed on third parties or buyers, he said the Cabinet views this issue seriously. “We constantly collaborate and engage with the Ministry of Home Affairs (KDN), including examining the need to amend relevant laws to ensure harsher penalties are imposed on cable theft offenders in the country. “There have been several instances where LRT (Light Rail Transit) operations were disrupted due to cable theft by syndicates; therefore, this matter (amending laws for heavier penalties) is crucial to ensuring we continue to safeguard public safety and the well-being of the people,” he said. description: 'Malaysia addresses its 40% daily food waste crisis through recycling initiatives while tightening laws against cable theft to protect public infrastructure.
full_text: 'Food Waste Forms Nearly 40% of Nation’s Daily Solid Waste, Says Minister. 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 5): Nearly 40% of the total 40,000 metric tonnes of solid waste generated in the country daily consists of food waste, according to Housing and Local Government Minister Nga Kor Ming. He said efforts to address this waste issue require the cooperation of all parties through a "whole-of-nation approach" involving both businesses and consumers to collectively change their attitudes and practices. “This is a form of waste. Food waste is not a crime, but it is a sin. It is a grave sin when edible food is simply thrown away,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat Monday. Nga said this when replying a question from Datuk Mumtaz Md Nawi (PN-Tumpat) regarding the latest developments in efforts to reduce waste sent to landfills and to increase recycling rates. Meanwhile, he expressed confidence that the ministry would achieve its target of exceeding a 40% recycling rate by the end of this year. Nga noted that under the "Trash to Cash" recycling programme, the total collection of recyclable materials between January and August exceeded 7.86 million kilogrammes (kg), with a sales value of over RM2.85 million. “Secondly, the zero-waste community initiative involving the establishment of 17 active zero-waste community centres during the same period has collected over 111,504kg of recyclable materials,” he said. Additionally, Nga said a school-based recycling competition, involving 1,680 schools, successfully collected 4.95 million kilogrammes of recyclable materials, which were sold for RM2.98 million. “Based on calculations of the total collected from 2018 to last year, we managed to gather nearly 20 million kilogrammes of recyclable items, generating proceeds exceeding RM10.22 million,” he said. Responding to a supplementary question from Mumtaz regarding the specific controls and enforcement actions implemented by the Ministry of Housing and Local Government concerning cable theft including penalties imposed on third parties or buyers, he said the Cabinet views this issue seriously. “We constantly collaborate and engage with the Ministry of Home Affairs (KDN), including examining the need to amend relevant laws to ensure harsher penalties are imposed on cable theft offenders in the country. “There have been several instances where LRT (Light Rail Transit) operations were disrupted due to cable theft by syndicates; therefore, this matter (amending laws for heavier penalties) is crucial to ensuring we continue to safeguard public safety and the well-being of the people,” he said. title: 'End ongoing violations of Orang Asli land rights in Pahang – 19 NGOs
body: 'We, the undersigned civil society organisations and individuals, are deeply concerned by the situation confronting the Orang Asli of Pahang in general, and of the communities of Tasek Bera in particular, who are facing eviction, harassment and arrest and are being treated as a scapegoat for ongoing deforestation. Violations in Tasek Bera In June 2026, about 20 Orang Asli villages in the Tasek Bera area received eviction notices from the Pahang Forestry Department, ordering them to vacate their settlements and farmland. These kampungs, including Kampung Kuala Serting, Kampung Lubuk Tiang, Kampung Tambangan, Kampung Lenguin, Kampung Gakuyah, Kampung Pathir, Kampung Limbahan, Kampung Mahang, Kampung Ibam and Kampung Buloh Nipis, lie within the Tasek Bera permanent forest reserve (hutan simpan kekal). In response, the communities acted collectively, erecting blockades to protect their customary lands and monitoring activities within their territories. On 14 September, officers from the Pahang State Forestry Department and Department of Wildlife arrived at Kampung Pathir, stating their intention to conduct land surveying. The communities refused them entry pending a resolution on the eviction notices, with Tok Batin Amir Noor Tan of Kampung Pathir calling for the eviction notices to be withdrawn. This standoff escalated, resulting in the arrest of five Orang Asli, four of them women, on the same day. They were subsequently released on 16 September. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Another similar incident involving police and communities within Tasek Bera also took place in Kampung Kuala Serting on 23 September. These recent developments are not an isolated case and form part of a growing trend of land grabs in Pahang. For example, outside Tasek Bera, on 9 February, 21 Orang Asli villagers from Kampung Jemeri in Rompin, Pahang, were detained by police following a complaint from a company claiming rights to develop land allegedly owned by the sultan of Pahang. According to a community statement, the sultan had [allegedly] obtained title to the 718-hectare oil palm plantation, developed by Orang Asli smallholders, less than a month earlier, on 26 January. The land in question forms part of the traditional territories of Jakun smallholders who had opened their smallholdings there 10-13 years ago. Orang Asli not driving deforestation Since early 2026, we have observed the development of a narrative in Pahang portraying the Orang Asli as groups that are scheming with outsiders to convert forest reserves into agricultural land. For example, while the above events were occurring in Tasek Bera, mainstream and state media repeatedly circulated claims that more than 7,000 hectares of forest within the Tasek Bera Ramsar site, which spans 38,446 hectares, had been illegally converted. This conversion was attributed to six Orang Asli families who allegedly used outsiders to exploit customary land rights in carrying out the encroachment. This narrative fails to accurately depict the drivers of deforestation in the state. A recent article by RimbaWatch found that at least 72,000 hectares of forest are under threat in Pahang, driven primarily by the expansion of monoculture industrial timber plantations in forest reserves, a programme supported by both the state and federal governments. Measured against this scale, traditional forest utilisation carried out by Orang Asli communities is minor. Yet it is their communities, not state and corporate drivers of deforestation, that are being singled out and blamed. Orang Asli traditional territories have existed for generations, predating independence and their later gazettement as timber production areas. Research has continuously shown that safeguarded Indigenous territories exhibit remarkable ecological resilience and biodiversity outcomes. Arrests of Orang Asli community members, ongoing harassment and the undue stress of receiving eviction notices or discovering that their land now belongs to outsiders all point to a troubling reality: as rights to their traditional territories are denied, the Orang Asli in Pahang are becoming outsiders on their own territories and scapegoated as drivers of widespread deforestation. Apex courts’ consistent rulings The Federal Court and Court of Appeal have repeatedly recognised that Orang Asli possess native customary land rights – a form of proprietary right protected under Article 13 of the Federal Constitution, provided a substantial connection to the land in question can be proven [Rosli Jendut & Ors v Agrobest (M) Sdn Bhd & Ors (2026)]. These rights pre-date both the Aboriginal Peoples Act 1954 and the National Land Code, and do not depend on any document of title. The rights are not limited to settlement areas. As the Federal Court in Rosli Jendut makes clear, these rights also extend to lands which are central to the Orang Asli’s cultural way of life, such as tombstones and grave sites. As such, despite the lack of gazettement and formal documents of title, the proprietary rights of Orang Asli communities in Tasek Bera over their traditional territories should be recognised and respected according to the Federal Court. Call to action The gaps between the judiciary and the executive are glaring and deeply concerning. While the courts have, time and again, affirmed the proprietary rights of the Orang Asli to their traditional territories, this recognition is not reflected by executive action. Communities like the Orang Asli in Tasek Bera, while actively fighting to protect their territories, are bearing the cost of this disconnect through evictions, arrests and the destruction of their lands. We urge the federal government to intervene immediately to safeguard the rights and wellbeing of the Orang Asli, as recognised by our Federal Courts and the Constitution. We call for an end to the misleading and negative portrayal of the Orang Asli community. Furthermore, we call for the following measures. - The Pahang state government must withdraw all eviction notices issued to the Orang Asli communities in Pahang, particularly those grounded solely on the claim that the communities are residing within permanent forest reserves. - The Pahang state government and their agencies must conduct genuine free, prior and informed consent consultation with affected communities for any decisions that will affect them, in line with Malaysia’s commitments under the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). - Suhakam must conduct an independent inquiry into the conduct of the Tasek Bera enforcement operations, and the findings made public and acted upon by the federal and Pahang state government without delay, vis-a-vis recommendations made in the 2013 National Inquiry on the Land Rights of Indigenous Peoples in Malaysia being adopted and implemented. - The Pahang state government and its agencies (eg Jakoa) must accelerate and make transparent the gazettement of Orang Asli traditional territories, with clear timelines for the villages still pending survey. - The federal government must halt the ongoing amendment process of the Orang Asli Act 1954 until legally binding recognition of traditional territories is guaranteed. title: 'BERNAMA - Maybank Group Sustainability Week 2026 Advances Net Zero Ambitions Through Capacity Building and Collective Action
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 25 (Bernama) -- Maybank recently organised the Maybank Group Sustainability Week (MGSW) 2026, a three-day programme held from 21 to 23 September 2026 at Menara Merdeka Maybank. Under the theme “Net Zero. From Commitment to Action”, MGSW 2026 focuses on advancing Maybank’s net zero journey through capacity building, sustainability awareness and capabilities, in line with the Group’s ROAR30 sustainability ambitions. MGSW 2026 saw Maybankers across the Group participate in two key events; ‘Net Zero Week’, the ‘Maybank Sustainability Practitioner Certification (MSPC) Open Day’ and ‘Grand Conferment Ceremony’, celebrating over 1,000 certified sustainability practitioners. title: 'Public Bank, Maybank and CIMB Among Eight Malaysian Banks on Forbes’ Global List
body: 'Eight Malaysian banks made Forbes’ inaugural ranking of the world’s top-performing banks in 2026. Public Bank ranked fifth in Tier 2, the highest position among Malaysia’s three entries in the category. Maybank placed 14th while CIMB Group Holdings ranked 35th. Tier 2 covers banks with assets from US$100 billion to US$500 billion. Hong Leong Financial Group ranked ninth in Tier 3 while RHB Bank placed 37th. The category covers banks with assets from US$50 billion to US$100 billion. Bank Rakyat placed 32nd in Tier 4 while AmBank Group ranked 68th. Tier 4 covers banks with assets from US$20 billion to US$50 billion. Alliance Bank Malaysia was the country’s sole Tier 5 entry and placed 90th. This category covers banks with assets from US$10 billion to US$20 billion. Forbes and Statista compiled the ranking using financial data, desk research and bank submissions. Unlike its survey-based bank rankings, the new list assesses financial performance. Banks were evaluated on profitability, earnings quality, resilience, asset quality and efficiency. Eligible institutions needed more than US$3 billion in assets, audited financial statements and at least three years of financial data. They were grouped into six tiers by asset size. The final list covered 500 banks across 89 countries, with no payment required to participate or be selected. title: 'Maybank emerges as top winner at inaugural Bursa Malaysia IR Awards 2026
body:
'

KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 7): Malayan Banking Bhd (KL:MAYBANK) emerged as the biggest winner at the inaugural Bursa Malaysia IR Awards 2026 that was held last Friday, sweeping home three awards including Best Financial Reporting and the flagship Best Company in IR.

Capping the hattrick win for the company was its sectoral win as Best Large-Cap company in IR for Financial Services while its president and group chief executive officer Datuk Seri Khairussaleh Ramli was named Best CEO in IR.

The awards honoured a total of 32 winners across eight main categories, celebrating public listed companies (PLCs) and investor relations professionals who have demonstrated a strong commitment to investor engagement, market communication and corporate transparency, Bursa said in a statement on Monday.

The eight categories are:

  1. Best Company in IR (overall)
  2. Best Financial Reporting
  3. Best Sustainability Communications
  4. Best IPO Company in IR
  5. Best CEO in IR
  6. Best CFO in IR
  7. Best Large-cap Company in IR by Sector (across 13 sectors)
  8. Best Mid/Small-cap Company in IR by Sector (across 13 sectors)

Other notable winners include Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA), which took home twin awards for Best Sustainability Communications and Best Large-cap Company in IR for Utilities, and Oriental Kopi Holdings Bhd (KL:KOPI), which was named Best IPO Company in IR. 

The other individual award — the Best CFO in IR — went to Malkit Singh Maan of Hong Leong Bank Bhd (KL:HLBANK).

Effective investor relations is important in strengthening the quality and competitiveness of Malaysia's listed companies, said Treasury secretary general Tan Sri Johan Mahmood Merican when delivering the keynote address at the awards celebrations.

“By communicating openly and consistently with investors, public listed companies enable better-informed investment decisions and demonstrate their commitment to transparency and accountability. As we continue enhancing the competitiveness and quality of Malaysia’s listed companies, effective investor engagement will remain an enabler of long-term value creation and sustainable market growth,” Johan said.

The inaugural awards aimed to recognise companies and professionals who are setting a high standard for transparency, engagement and market communication, said Bursa CEO Datuk Fad'l Mohamed.

"By spotlighting these practices, we hope to encourage more listed companies to strengthen their investor relations capabilities and help raise standards of investor engagement across the market," he said.

He also noted that there is considerable opportunity to strengthen IR capabilities across the market and enhance issuer-investor engagement across the market.

Based on Bursa's research, only 32% of listed companies have a dedicated internal IR function while 17% outsource the function and 51% operate without any formal IR structure.

The exchange operator and regulator said it has been building IR capabilities in the capital market through IR4U by providing practical guidance and learning opportunities for PLCs, which saw the participation of about 690 listed companies throughout 2024 and 2025.

These efforts are complemented by MY Value Up, the national capital market initiative jointly launched by the Securities Commission Malaysia and Bursa to encourage companies to strengthen fundamentals while articulating their strategies and priorities more clearly to the market.

The complete list of award winners will be featured in a special pullout in The Edge Malaysia weekly.
