As we continue enhancing the competitiveness and quality of Malaysia’s listed companies, effective investor engagement will remain an enabler of long-term value creation and sustainable market growth,” Johan said.

The inaugural awards aimed to recognise companies and professionals who are setting a high standard for transparency, engagement and market communication, said Bursa CEO Datuk Fad'l Mohamed.

"By spotlighting these practices, we hope to encourage more listed companies to strengthen their investor relations capabilities and help raise standards of investor engagement across the market," he said.

He also noted that there is considerable opportunity to strengthen IR capabilities across the market and enhance issuer-investor engagement across the market.

Based on Bursa's research, only 32% of listed companies have a dedicated internal IR function while 17% outsource the function and 51% operate without any formal IR structure.

The exchange operator and regulator said it has been building IR capabilities in the capital market through IR4U by providing practical guidance and learning opportunities for PLCs, which saw the participation of about 690 listed companies throughout 2024 and 2025.

These efforts are complemented by MY Value Up, the national capital market initiative jointly launched by the Securities Commission Malaysia and Bursa to encourage companies to strengthen fundamentals while articulating their strategies and priorities more clearly to the market.

The complete list of award winners will be featured in a special pullout in The Edge Malaysia weekly.

title: 'AG cautions on use of AI, effective human oversight is still essential
body:
'

KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): While the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has been used extensively and relied upon in the last few years, Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar cautioned for the need for human oversight in its usage.

Dusuki said there is no doubt that AI offers significant opportunities in various sectors.

For instance, he said, in healthcare, it can assist clinical judgement while in the corporate sphere, it can support decision-making, improve efficiency, and help professionals process increasingly complex information.

“But as our reliance on these systems grows, so, too, does the importance of understanding how they are used and how they are governed. We need to ask some very practical questions: How reliable is the information produced by an AI system? What are the limits of its capabilities? Who is responsible for checking its output?” he said.

He questioned what would happen when the AI system does not perform as expected.

“These are not merely questions about technology. They are questions of governance, professional responsibility, and human oversight. Increasingly, they may also have consequences for legal liability and insurance.

“For any institution adopting AI, it is therefore important to understand why the technology is being used, what risks may arise from its use, and what safeguards are necessary. Technology may assist professional judgement, but effective human oversight remains essential,” he reminded.

Dusuki was delivering his keynote address at the Inaugural Financial Lines Forum at a hotel here.

Lembaga Tabung Haji chairman and RHB Bank founder Tan Sri Abdul Rashid Hussin

Also present were Lembaga Tabung Haji chairman and RHB Bank founder Tan Sri Abdul Rashid Hussin, who delivered a special address, and former Federal Court judge Tan Sri Zainun Ali, former Chief Judge of Malaya Tan Sri Hasnah Mohamed Hashim, as well as former and current judges.

The AG said that while there are continuing issues in the usage of AI, there is a need to use it responsibly.

Dusuki said the use of AI requires engagement among those who develop the technology, those who deploy it, those who rely on it, and those who assess and manage the risks associated with its use.

Hence, he welcomed the organisation of such a forum like the Financial Lines Forum as it brings together legal professionals, healthcare practitioners, corporate leaders, insurers, brokers, and other stakeholders.

“We have an opportunity to learn from one another, to better understand the risks and opportunities before us, and to consider how our respective professions can respond responsibly to a rapidly changing environment.

“Ultimately, the question is not simply what artificial intelligence can do. The more important question is, how we, as professionals, choose to use it responsibly,” he added.

The one-day forum gathers medical experts, insurers, lawyers, and judges in exchanging views on medical negligence, governance, and AI.

title: 'PMCK Expands Beyond Hospitals as Maybank Maintains BUY With RM0.35 Target Price
body: 'PMCK Bhd is entering a new phase of growth as the healthcare group expands beyond its core hospital operations into the medical consumables business. Maybank Investment Bank remains positive on the company, maintaining its BUY recommendation with an unchanged target price of RM0.35, compared with PMCK’s share price of RM0.195 in the report, implying potential upside of about 79%. A major highlight is PMCK’s proposed RM52.8 million acquisition of Marpoliq Sdn Bhd and Derberg Sdn Bhd, two medical consumables suppliers. The acquisition will broaden PMCK’s healthcare ecosystem from hospital services into sourcing and distribution of disposable medical devices, respiratory and airway products, feeding supplies, incontinence pads and other hospital and home-care accessories. Completion is targeted by 1Q27. Maybank views the deal positively because medical consumables provide recurring and higher-margin income while giving PMCK exposure to both government and private hospitals. Importantly, the acquisition comes with a RM3 million annual profit-after-tax guarantee for FY27E and FY28E. The deal is valued at just 7.2x P/E and 4.9x EV/EBITDA, significantly below the average valuations of Bursa-listed medical supply peers. The earnings impact could also be meaningful. Maybank estimates the acquisitions could increase PMCK’s FY27E core net profit from RM13.0 million to RM16.8 million, representing a 29.4% uplift after accounting for the acquired companies’ earnings contribution and additional interest expenses. Both businesses also enjoy stronger profitability, with FY26 PAT margins of 21.6% for Marpoliq and 29.1% for Derberg, compared with PMCK’s existing margin of around 12%. Beyond the acquisition, PMCK has an established healthcare footprint in northern Malaysia. It has operated PMC Alor Setar since 1995, while Kedah and Perlis remain relatively underserved in terms of private hospital beds. Another major catalyst is the upcoming 90-bed PMC Kulim hospital, targeted for 1QCY28, which should expand capacity and increase patient throughput. Looking ahead, Maybank forecasts PMCK’s revenue rising from RM107.1 million in FY27E to RM207.2 million in FY29E, while core net profit is projected to increase from RM13.6 million to RM19.8 million. With hospital expansion, growing patient volumes and the move into higher-margin medical consumables, PMCK is building multiple growth engines that could strengthen its longer-term earnings profile.

title: 'Bursa Ends Lower, FBM KLCI Sheds 20.81 Points As Selling Pressure Persists
body: 'Bursa Malaysia closed broadly lower on Oct 1, with the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) falling 20.81 points, or 1.26%, to 1,630.36 as continued selling pressure tracked a mixed and cautious Wall Street session overnight.  The benchmark index, which closed at 1,651.17 on Sept 30, traded between 1,630.10 and 1,649.87 during the day.  Weakness extended across the broader market. The FBM 70 dropped 215.69 points, or 1.23%, to 17,358.98, while the F4GBM fell 12.12 points, or 1.22%, to 984.34.  The FBM Emas declined 148.49 points, or 1.21%, to 12,143.53, while the FBM Shariah lost 163.34 points, or 1.34%, to 12,013.01.  Heavyweight counters were mostly lower. Maybank slipped four sen to RM9.95, Public Bank fell three sen to RM4.67 and CIMB shed 10 sen to RM7.69. Tenaga Nasional declined six sen to RM12.90, while IHH Healthcare lost 13 sen to RM7.70.  Among the most actively traded stocks, Zetrix AI Bhd added 0.5 sen to 16.5 sen on 188.38 million shares, while VS Industry Bhd fell one sen to 27 sen.  JAKS Resources Bhd dropped 2.5 sen to 18 sen, newly ACE Market listed GB Bond Holdings Bhd slid 4.5 sen to 20.5 sen, while HHRG Bhd gained 0.5 sen to 16.5 sen.  Trading activity eased, with turnover falling to 3.1 billion units worth RM2.7 billion, from 3.63 billion units valued at RM3.62 billion on Sept 30.

title: 'Benign inflation keeps OPR outlook intact: CIMB Securities
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's inflation may remain benign despite firmer monthly price increases and rising food and electricity costs, according to CIMB Securities. The research house said headline inflation rose to 1.9 per cent year-on-year (YoY) in August from 1.8 per cent in July, while core inflation eased to 1.7 per cent from 1.8 per cent, largely due to favourable base effects in information and communication. However, both headline and core prices rose 0.3 per cent month-on-month (MoM), compared with no change in July, indicating firmer sequential price momentum. "Nonetheless, other indicators in our inflation monitor, including the persistence signal, showed no signs of a pickup in underlying price pressures," CIMB Securities said in a research note. It said food-at-home inflation accelerated to 1.4 per cent YoY from 1.2 per cent, with egg prices rising 5.9 per cent and vegetable prices increasing 2.8 per cent. Electricity inflation also climbed to 3.6 per cent from 2.2 per cent following a higher imbalance cost pass-through surcharge in August. However, the expanded electricity surcharge exemption for Peninsular Malaysia households consuming up to 800kWh monthly, from 600kWh previously, should help contain further pressure between September and December. CIMB Securities expects headline inflation to remain around 1.9 per cent to two per cent in September, with the broader outlook staying manageable. "The softer core reading and still-contained underlying price pressures support our Bank Negara Malaysia policy outlook," it said, maintaining its expectation for the overnight policy rate to remain at 2.75 per cent at the central bank's Monetary Policy Committee meeting in November. On trade, CIMB Securities said August exports surged 45.5 per cent YoY, driven mainly by electrical and electronics and other manufactured goods. However, it cautioned that the strength remained concentrated, while softer momentum in non-E&E and non-petroleum manufacturing exports and potential US semiconductor tariffs continued to pose risks to the growth outlook.

title: 'Samaiden Reveals RM238 Mil Contract Value for LSS5+ Solar Project
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Renewable energy solutions provider Samaiden Group Bhd (KL:SAMAIDEN) said its contracts to undertake works for a 99.99-megawatt (MW) Large Scale Solar 5+ (LSS5+) project are worth RM238 million. The group disclosed the contract value in a Bursa Malaysia filing on Tuesday, four days after announcing the contracts without revealing their value due to confidentiality restrictions. Samaiden's wholly-owned subsidiary Samaiden Sdn Bhd had on Oct 2 entered into a works contract and a contract for the supply of solar components with Syarikat Pembenaan Yeoh Tiong Lay Sdn Bhd (YTL Construction), the construction unit of YTL Corporation Bhd (KL:YTL). YTL Construction, which is the project's main contractor, appointed Samaiden to undertake engineering, construction and commissioning works, as well as the procurement and supply of solar components for the 99.99MW alternating-current solar photovoltaic plant. The project is among the LSS5+ projects approved by the Energy Commission in September 2025. Samaiden said the scope of works includes the supply and delivery of materials, design, engineering, construction, testing and completion of the solar photovoltaic facility, with work to commence upon the issuance of a notice to proceed. The group had earlier posted record annual earnings and revenue for the financial year ended June 30, 2026 (FY2026), its strongest performance since listing in 2020. Net profit for FY2026 surged 93.3% to RM39.07 million from RM20.21 million a year earlier, while revenue rose 3.1% to RM364.5 million from RM353.47 million. The group's order book stood at RM435.8 million as at end-June. Samaiden shares fell seven sen or 2.19% to close at RM3.12 on Tuesday, valuing the group at RM1.75 billion. Year to date, however, the counter is up 124.5%. title: 'Apa yang mesti berubah sebelum pelajar lain dicederakan?/ What must change before another child is hurt?
body: '[ENGLISH VERSION BELOW] Kematian Muhammad ldlan Fareeq Shahril, 14 tahun, meninggalkan sebuah keluarga dalam kesedihan dan ibu bapa di seluruh Malaysia dengan satu pertanyaan yang amat membimbangkan: adakah anak saya selamat di asrama sekolah? Bagi pihak Children’s Protection Society Malaysia (CPSM), saya merakamkan ucapan takziah yang sedalam-dalamnya kepada ibu bapa dan keluarga Muhammad ldlan. Tiada kata-kata yang dapat meringankan kehilangan mereka. Mereka berhak mendapat ruang untuk berduka, dan jawapan yang benar serta keadilan. Kami mengambil maklum bahawa Menteri Pendidikan Fadhlina Sidek telah bertemu dengan keluarga dan warga sekolah serta mengarahkan audit segera. Kami menyambut baik jaminan beliau bahawa tiada sesiapa akan dilindungi sekiranya salah laku terbukti. Polis mesti diberi ruang untuk menentukan fakta, termasuk punca dan keadaan yang membawa kepada kematian Muhammad ldlan. Dakwaan tidak boleh dianggap sebagai dapatan, dan pelajar yang terlibat tidak wajar dihakimi oleh masyarakat sebelum siasatan selesai. Namun, siasatan terhadap satu kejadian tidak boleh menjadi noktah kepada perkara ini. Audit tersebut perlu menjawab soalan yang lebih sukar: adakah terdapat kebimbangan yang timbul sebelum kematian Muhammad ldlan, dan adakah pihak asrama mempunyai cara yang berkesan untuk mengenal pasti serta menanganinya? Soalan ini perlu diteliti tanpa membuat andaian tentang apa yang berlaku dalam kes ini. Apabila seorang pelajar tinggal di asrama, pihak sekolah memikul tanggungjawab menjaganya pada waktu ibu bapanya tidak dapat melihat keadaannya sendiri. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Tanggungjawab itu melangkaui daftar penghuni dan peraturan yang ditampal pada papan kenyataan semata-mata. la memerlukan orang dewasa yang mengenali pelajar, menyedari perubahan tingkah laku, mengambil tindakan apabila kebimbangan dibangkitkan dan bertanggungjawab terhadap keselamatan mereka selepas waktu persekolahan. Tiada pelajar berhak menguatkuasakan disiplin dengan kekerasan. Jika seorang pelajar disyaki melanggar peraturan, sama ada berkaitan dengan vape, barang yang hilang, sikap tidak menghormati orang lain atau apa-apa perkara sekalipun, urusan itu mesti dikendalikan oleh orang dewasa yang bertanggungjawab. Pelajar tidak boleh ditampar, dipukul, ditahan secara paksa, diugut atau dikenakan hukuman yang dikendalikan oleh pelajar lain. Sesiapa yang melihat sesuatu masalah hendaklah melaporkannya kepada warden atau guru disiplin. Tiada tempat bagi pelajar yang melantik diri mereka sendiri sebagai penguat kuasa di dormitori, asrama atau sekolah. Oleh itu, CPSM menyeru Kementerian Pendidikan supaya menggunakan audit semasa sebagai permulaan kepada semakan keselamatan asrama yang jelas dan mempunyai tempoh pelaksanaan yang ditetapkan. Semakan itu perlu merangkumi perkara berikut. Pertama, teliti sama ada tanda amaran terlepas pandang. Penyiasat dan pasukan audit perlu meneliti aduan terdahulu, laporan tidak rasmi, permintaan untuk bertukar bilik, kecederaan yang tidak dapat dijelaskan, ketidakhadiran, perubahan tingkah laku dan kebimbangan yang dibangkitkan oleh ibu bapa, sekiranya maklumat tersebut wujud. Mereka perlu mengenal pasti siapa yang menerima setiap maklumat, tindakan yang diambil dan sama ada keadaan pelajar berkenaan disusuli. Jika tiada aduan direkodkan, hal itu perlu dinilai secara bersama satu lagi persoalan: adakah pelajar mempunyai saluran yang selamat dan boleh dipercayai untuk bersuara? Kedua, pastikan penyeliaan orang dewasa ada pada waktu dan tempat pelajar memerlukannya. Warden sukar menjalankan pengawasan yang rapi jika mereka perlu menjaga terlalu ramai pelajar, beberapa bangunan atau terlalu banyak tugas serentak. Kementerian perlu menyemak jumlah petugas asrama, liputan pada waktu malam, serah tugas dan tatacara mendapatkan bantuan apabila sesuatu kejadian berlaku. Setiap asrama perlu mempunyai petugas yang jelas dikenalpasti sedang bertugas, pengganti apabila petugas tersebut tiada, serta rekod kebimbangan yang dibangkitkan dan tindakan yang diambil yang disimpan dengan selamat. Ketiga, sediakan saluran aduan yang diyakini pelajar. Seorang pelajar perlu boleh bercakap secara sulit dengan lebih daripada seorang petugas yang ditetapkan, termasuk seseorang di luar rantaian pengurusan harian asrama. lbu bapa juga mesti tahu siapa yang boleh dihubungi. Laporan mengenai keganasan atau ugutan perlu mendapat respons segera, penilaian terhadap keselamatan pelajar, perlindungan daripada tindakan balas dan tindakan susulan. Pelajar perlu diberitahu dengan jelas bahawa melaporkan perbuatan yang memudaratkan orang lain ialah tindakan berani, bukannya perbuatan tidak setia kepada rakan. Keempat, fahami keperluan setiap pelajar apabila mereka mula tinggal di asrama. Pihak sekolah perlu berbincang dengan pelajar dan ibu bapa tentang penyesuaian kepada kehidupan berasrama, sebarang kebimbangan keselamatan yang pernah timbul, dan sokongan yang mungkin diperlukan. Jika sesuatu kebimbangan memerlukan penilaian lanjut, profesional yang berkelayakan perlu dilibatkan. Maklumat yang diperoleh mesti dirahsiakan dan digunakan untuk merancang sokongan serta penyeliaan yang sesuai, bukan untuk melabel seorang pelajar atau menafikan aksesnya kepada pendidikan berdasarkan andaian yang belum diuji. Kelima, jadikan larangan terhadap keganasan suatu amalan yang benar-benar dilaksanakan. Pengetua, warden, guru disiplin, kaunselor dan, jika berkaitan, ustaz atau pendidik agama lain perlu menyampaikan mesej yang sama secara konsisten. Perhimpunan mingguan dan pertemuan di asrama boleh digunakan untuk membincangkan batas pergaulan, tekanan rakan sebaya, cara menegur dengan hormat dan cara mendapatkan bantuan. Toleransi sitar terhadap keganasan mesti diterjemahkan melalui tindakan yang konsisten: setiap laporan diambil serius, pelajar yang terlibat dilindungi, fakta ditentukan dan tindakan diambil secara adil. Arahan kepada pelajar mesti jelas: jangan gunakan kekerasan terhadap pelajar lain; laporkan masalah kepada orang dewasa; dan jika melihat kejadian yang membahayakan seseorang, dapatkan bantuan dengan segera tanpa meletakkan diri sendiri dalam bahaya. Keenam, laksanakan langkah keselamatan yang praktikal. Kementerian perlu menyemak peraturan keselamatan di asrama sekolah dan mengenal pasti kawasan bersama yang sesuai untuk pemantauan CCTV, dengan keutamaan kepada tempat yang mungkin mendedahkan pelajar kepada risiko apabila penyeliaan orang dewasa terhad. Penggunaan kamera mesti menghormati privasi pelajar dan tidak boleh menggantikan kehadiran orang dewasa yang peka. Setiap sistem perlu mempunyai petugas yang bertanggungjawab memastikan ia berfungsi, bertindak apabila kejadian dilaporkan dan menyimpan rakaman berkaitan sebelum rakaman itu terpadam secara automatik. Akses kepada rakaman hendaklah dihadkan dan direkodkan, manakala rakaman yang relevan perlu diserahkan segera kepada penyiasat melalui saluran yang betul dengan perlindungan terhadap identiti pelajar yang dirakam. Kebertanggungjawaban mesti melangkaui kes ini. Persoalan yang timbul daripada kematian ini mesti membawa kepada tindakan yang dapat dilihat oleh ibu bapa dan pelajar. Kementerian perlu menerbitkan dapatan utama audit sebaik sahaja hal itu dapat dilakukan tanpa menjejaskan siasatan polis atau privasi pelajar yang terlibat. Kementerian juga perlu menyatakan perkara yang akan diperbetulkan, pegawai yang bertanggungjawab dan tarikh setiap tindakan perlu diselesaikan. Semakan yang sama hendaklah diperluas ke asrama lain, dengan kemajuan pelaksanaannya dimaklumkan kepada umum. Mesej tentang keganasan yang diterima golongan muda di luar sekolah juga wajar diberi perhatian. Penggiat industri kreatif dan badan kawal selia perlu meneliti cara perbuatan membuli dipaparkan kepada penonton muda, khususnya apabila ugutan dan kekerasan digambarkan seolah-olah memberikan kuasa atau tidak membawa akibat. Pandangan golongan muda tentang mesej yang mereka fahami daripada kandungan yang ditonton patut didengar. Gambaran dalam karya kreatif tidak boleh dijadikan penjelasan bagi kematian Muhammad ldlan; fakta kes ini mesti ditentukan oleh penyiasat. Tanggungjawab menjaga keselamatan pelajar tetap terletak pada orang dewasa dan institusi yang diamanahkan menjaga mereka. lbu bapa menyerahkan anak kepada sekolah untuk dijaga, bukan semata-mata untuk memperoleh keputusan peperiksaan. Keluarga Muhammad ldlan berhak mengetahui kebenaran tentang apa yang berlaku. Setiap pelajar yang tinggal di asrama berhak mempunyai orang dewasa yang boleh dipercayai untuk diminta pertolongan, serta sistem yang bertindak sebelum sesuatu kemudaratan tidak lagi dapat dihalang. – CPSM Dato’ Seri Nazir Ariff ialah presiden Children’s Protection Society Malaysia. English version A child died in a school hostel. What must change before another child is hurt? The death of 14-year-old Muhammad ldlan Fareeq Shahril has left a family grieving and parents across Malaysia asking a painful question: is my child safe in a school hostel? On behalf of the Children’s Protection Society Malaysia (CPSM), I extend our deepest condolences to Muhammad ldlan’s parents and family. No statement can lessen their loss. They deserve compassion, privacy, truthful answers and justice. We acknowledge that Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek met the family and school community and directed an immediate audit. We welcome her assurance that no one will be protected if wrongdoing is established. The police must be allowed to establish the facts, including the cause and circumstances of Muhammad ldlan’s death. We must not turn an allegation into a finding or expose the children involved to public judgement before the investigation is complete. But an investigation into one incident cannot be the end of the matter. An audit must answer a harder question: were there concerns before Muhammad ldlan’s death, and did the hostel have a reliable way to recognise and respond to them? That question must be asked without presuming what happened in this case. A hostel takes responsibility for children during the hours when their parents cannot see them. That responsibility extends beyond a register of occupants and a set of rules on a noticeboard. It requires adults who know the children to notice changes in behaviour, respond to concerns and remain accountable for what happens after classes end. No student has the authority to enforce discipline by force. If a student is suspected of breaking a rule, whether it concerns vaping, a missing item, disrespect or anything else, the matter belongs with responsible adults. A child must never be slapped, struck, restrained, threatened or subjected to a punishment devised by other students. A student who sees a problem should report it to a warden or disciplinary teacher. There is no place for self-appointed enforcers in a dormitory, hostel or school. The CPSM therefore calls on the Ministry of Education to use the current audit to begin a clear, time-bound review of hostel safety. That review should address the following. First, find out whether warning signs were missed. Investigators and auditors should examine earlier complaints, informal reports, requests to change rooms, unexplained injuries, absences, changes in behaviour and concerns raised by parents, where such information exists. They should establish who received each concern, what action followed, and whether anyone checked back with the child. A finding that no complaints were recorded would need to be considered alongside whether children had a safe and credible way to speak up. Second, put adult supervision where and when children need it. Wardens cannot provide careful oversight if they are responsible for too many students, buildings or duties at once. The ministry should review hostel staffing, night coverage, handovers and escalation arrangements. Every hostel should have an identifiable adult on duty, a clear arrangement for cover when that adult is unavailable, and a secure record of concerns raised and action taken. '[ENGLISH VERSION BELOW] Kematian Muhammad ldlan Fareeq Shahril, 14 tahun, meninggalkan sebuah keluarga dalam kesedihan dan ibu bapa di seluruh Malaysia dengan satu pertanyaan yang amat membimbangkan: adakah anak saya selamat di asrama sekolah? Bagi pihak Children’s Protection Society Malaysia (CPSM), saya merakamkan ucapan takziah yang sedalam-dalamnya kepada ibu bapa dan keluarga Muhammad ldlan. Tiada kata-kata yang dapat meringankan kehilangan mereka. Mereka berhak mendapat ruang untuk berduka, dan jawapan yang benar serta keadilan. Kami mengambil maklum bahawa Menteri Pendidikan Fadhlina Sidek telah bertemu dengan keluarga dan warga sekolah serta mengarahkan audit segera. Kami menyambut baik jaminan beliau bahawa tiada sesiapa akan dilindungi sekiranya salah laku terbukti. Polis mesti diberi ruang untuk menentukan fakta, termasuk punca dan keadaan yang membawa kepada kematian Muhammad ldlan. Dakwaan tidak boleh dianggap sebagai dapatan, dan pelajar yang terlibat tidak wajar dihakimi oleh masyarakat sebelum siasatan selesai. Namun, siasatan terhadap satu kejadian tidak boleh menjadi noktah kepada perkara ini. Audit tersebut perlu menjawab soalan yang lebih sukar: adakah terdapat kebimbangan yang timbul sebelum kematian Muhammad ldlan, dan adakah pihak asrama mempunyai cara yang berkesan untuk mengenal pasti serta menanganinya? Soalan ini perlu diteliti tanpa membuat andaian tentang apa yang berlaku dalam kes ini. Apabila seorang pelajar tinggal di asrama, pihak sekolah memikul tanggungjawab menjaganya pada waktu ibu bapanya tidak dapat melihat keadaannya sendiri. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Tanggungjawab itu melangkaui daftar penghuni dan peraturan yang ditampal pada papan kenyataan semata-mata. la memerlukan orang dewasa yang mengenali pelajar, menyedari perubahan tingkah laku, mengambil tindakan apabila kebimbangan dibangkitkan dan bertanggungjawab terhadap keselamatan mereka selepas waktu persekolahan. Tiada pelajar berhak menguatkuasakan disiplin dengan kekerasan. Jika seorang pelajar disyaki melanggar peraturan, sama ada berkaitan dengan vape, barang yang hilang, sikap tidak menghormati orang lain atau apa-apa perkara sekalipun, urusan itu mesti dikendalikan oleh orang dewasa yang bertanggungjawab. Pelajar tidak boleh ditampar, dipukul, ditahan secara paksa, diugut atau dikenakan hukuman yang dikendalikan oleh pelajar lain. Sesiapa yang melihat sesuatu masalah hendaklah melaporkannya kepada warden atau guru disiplin. Tiada tempat bagi pelajar yang melantik diri mereka sendiri sebagai penguat kuasa di dormitori, asrama atau sekolah. Oleh itu, CPSM menyeru Kementerian Pendidikan supaya menggunakan audit semasa sebagai permulaan kepada semakan keselamatan asrama yang jelas dan mempunyai tempoh pelaksanaan yang ditetapkan. Semakan itu perlu merangkumi perkara berikut. Pertama, teliti sama ada tanda amaran terlepas pandang. Penyiasat dan pasukan audit perlu meneliti aduan terdahulu, laporan tidak rasmi, permintaan untuk bertukar bilik, kecederaan yang tidak dapat dijelaskan, ketidakhadiran, perubahan tingkah laku dan kebimbangan yang dibangkitkan oleh ibu bapa, sekiranya maklumat tersebut wujud. Mereka perlu mengenal pasti siapa yang menerima setiap maklumat, tindakan yang diambil dan sama ada keadaan pelajar berkenaan disusuli. Jika tiada aduan direkodkan, hal itu perlu dinilai secara bersama satu lagi persoalan: adakah pelajar mempunyai saluran yang selamat dan boleh dipercayai untuk bersuara? Kedua, pastikan penyeliaan orang dewasa ada pada waktu dan tempat pelajar memerlukannya. Warden sukar menjalankan pengawasan yang rapi jika mereka perlu menjaga terlalu ramai pelajar, beberapa bangunan atau terlalu banyak tugas serentak. Kementerian perlu menyemak jumlah petugas asrama, liputan pada waktu malam, serah tugas dan tatacara mendapatkan bantuan apabila sesuatu kejadian berlaku. Setiap asrama perlu mempunyai petugas yang jelas dikenalpasti sedang bertugas, pengganti apabila petugas tersebut tiada, serta rekod kebimbangan yang dibangkitkan dan tindakan yang diambil yang disimpan dengan selamat. Ketiga, sediakan saluran aduan yang diyakini pelajar. Seorang pelajar perlu boleh bercakap secara sulit dengan lebih daripada seorang petugas yang ditetapkan, termasuk seseorang di luar rantaian pengurusan harian asrama. lbu bapa juga mesti tahu siapa yang boleh dihubungi. Laporan mengenai keganasan atau ugutan perlu mendapat respons segera, penilaian terhadap keselamatan pelajar, perlindungan daripada tindakan balas dan tindakan susulan. Pelajar perlu diberitahu dengan jelas bahawa melaporkan perbuatan yang memudaratkan orang lain ialah tindakan berani, bukannya perbuatan tidak setia kepada rakan. Keempat, fahami keperluan setiap pelajar apabila mereka mula tinggal di asrama. Pihak sekolah perlu berbincang dengan pelajar dan ibu bapa tentang penyesuaian kepada kehidupan berasrama, sebarang kebimbangan keselamatan yang pernah timbul, dan sokongan yang mungkin diperlukan. Jika sesuatu kebimbangan memerlukan penilaian lanjut, profesional yang berkelayakan perlu dilibatkan. Maklumat yang diperoleh mesti dirahsiakan dan digunakan untuk merancang sokongan serta penyeliaan yang sesuai, bukan untuk melabel seorang pelajar atau menafikan aksesnya kepada pendidikan berdasarkan andaian yang belum diuji. Pengetua, warden, guru disiplin, kaunselor dan, jika berkaitan, ustaz atau pendidik agama lain perlu menyampaikan mesej yang sama secara konsisten. Perhimpunan mingguan dan pertemuan di asrama boleh digunakan untuk membincangkan batas pergaulan, tekanan rakan sebaya, cara menegur dengan hormat dan cara mendapatkan bantuan. Keenam, laksanakan langkah keselamatan yang praktikal. Penggunaan kamera mesti menghormati privasi pelajar dan tidak boleh menggantikan kehadiran orang dewasa yang peka. Setiap sistem perlu mempunyai petugas yang bertanggungjawab memastikan ia berfungsi, bertindak apabila kejadian dilaporkan dan menyimpan rakaman berkaitan sebelum rakaman itu terpadam secara automatik. Akses kepada rakaman hendaklah dihadkan dan direkodkan, manakala rakaman yang relevan perlu diserahkan segera kepada penyiasat melalui saluran yang betul dengan perlindungan terhadap identiti pelajar yang dirakam. Kebertanggungjawaban mesti melangkaui kes ini. Persoalan yang timbul daripada kematian ini mesti membawa kepada tindakan yang dapat dilihat oleh ibu bapa dan pelajar. Kementerian perlu menerbitkan dapatan utama audit sebaik sahaja hal itu dapat dilakukan tanpa menjejaskan siasatan polis atau privasi pelajar yang terlibat. Kementerian juga perlu menyatakan perkara yang akan diperbetulkan, pegawai yang bertanggungjawab dan tarikh setiap tindakan perlu diselesaikan. Semakan yang sama hendaklah diperluas ke asrama lain, dengan kemajuan pelaksanaannya dimaklumkan kepada umum. Mesej tentang keganasan yang diterima golongan muda di luar sekolah juga wajar diberi perhatian. Penggiat industri kreatif dan badan kawal selia perlu meneliti cara perbuatan membuli dipaparkan kepada penonton muda, khususnya apabila ugutan dan kekerasan digambarkan seolah-olah memberikan kuasa atau tidak membawa akibat. Pandangan golongan muda tentang mesej yang mereka fahami daripada kandungan yang ditonton patut didengar. Gambaran dalam karya kreatif tidak boleh dijadikan penjelasan bagi kematian Muhammad ldlan; fakta kes ini mesti ditentukan oleh penyiasat. Tanggungjawab menjaga keselamatan pelajar tetap terletak pada orang dewasa dan institusi yang diamanahkan menjaga mereka. lbu bapa menyerahkan anak kepada sekolah untuk dijaga, bukan semata-mata untuk memperoleh keputusan peperiksaan. Keluarga Muhammad ldlan berhak mengetahui kebenaran tentang apa yang berlaku. Setiap pelajar yang tinggal di asrama berhak mempunyai orang dewasa yang boleh dipercayai untuk diminta pertolongan, serta sistem yang bertindak sebelum sesuatu kemudaratan tidak lagi dapat dihalang. – CPSM Dato’ Seri Nazir Ariff ialah presiden Children’s Protection Society Malaysia. The death of 14-year-old Muhammad ldlan Fareeq Shahril has left a family grieving and parents across Malaysia asking a painful question: is my child safe in a school hostel? On behalf of the Children’s Protection Society Malaysia (CPSM), I extend our deepest condolences to Muhammad ldlan’s parents and family. No statement can lessen their loss. They deserve compassion, privacy, truthful answers and justice. We acknowledge that Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek met the family and school community and directed an immediate audit. We welcome her assurance that no one will be protected if wrongdoing is established. The police must be allowed to establish the facts, including the cause and circumstances of Muhammad ldlan’s death. We must not turn an allegation into a finding or expose the children involved to public judgement before the investigation is complete. But an investigation into one incident cannot be the end of the matter. An audit must answer a harder question: were there concerns before Muhammad ldlan’s death, and did the hostel have a reliable way to recognise and respond to them? That question must be asked without presuming what happened in this case. A hostel takes responsibility for children during the hours when their parents cannot see them. That responsibility extends beyond a register of occupants and a set of rules on a noticeboard. It requires adults who know the children to notice changes in behaviour, respond to concerns and remain accountable for what happens after classes end. No student has the authority to enforce discipline by force. If a student is suspected of breaking a rule, whether it concerns vaping, a missing item, disrespect or anything else, the matter belongs with responsible adults. A child must never be slapped, struck, restrained, threatened or subjected to a punishment devised by other students. A student who sees a problem should report it to a warden or disciplinary teacher. There is no place for self-appointed enforcers in a dormitory, hostel or school. The CPSM therefore calls on the Ministry of Education to use the current audit to begin a clear, time-bound review of hostel safety. That review should address the following. First, find out whether warning signs were missed. Investigators and auditors should examine earlier complaints, informal reports, requests to change rooms, unexplained injuries, absences, changes in behaviour and concerns raised by parents, where such information exists. They should establish who received each concern, what action followed, and whether anyone checked back with the child. A finding that no complaints were recorded would need to be considered alongside whether children had a safe and credible way to speak up. Second, put adult supervision where and when children need it. Wardens cannot provide careful oversight if they are responsible for too many students, buildings or duties at once. The ministry should review hostel staffing, night coverage, handovers and escalation arrangements. Parents must know whom to contact. Reports involving violence or threats must receive a prompt response, an assessment of the child’s immediate safety, protection against retaliation and follow-up. Where a concern warrants further assessment, a qualified professional should be involved. Information gathered must be kept confidential and used to plan appropriate support and supervision, not to label a child or deny access to education on the basis of an untested assumption. Fifth, make the rule against violence a living practice. Principals, wardens, disciplinary teachers, counsellors and, where relevant, ustaz or other religious educators should reinforce the same message. Weekly assemblies and hostel meetings can provide regular opportunities to discuss boundaries, peer pressure, respectful correction and how to seek help. The ministry should review security arrangements across school hostels and identify shared areas where CCTV would strengthen oversight, with priority given to locations where children may be particularly vulnerable and adult supervision is limited. title: 'Opinion: When audit opinions meet uncertain numbers
body: 'Opinion: When audit opinions meet uncertain numbers Two lawsuits filed within days of each other in late July and early August have renewed a question that matters to every investor. When financial statements rest on estimates that could go either way, what does a “clean” audit opinion actually guarantee? The liquidators of Serba Dinamik Holdings Bhd are seeking at least RM1.56 billion from KPMG, alleging that unqualified opinions between FY2016 and FY2019 failed to detect revenue overstatements of up to 87%. The suit claims the misstatements would have been uncovered earlier, before the group paid RM1.795 billion in dividends, which the claim links to the alleged audit failures. Around the same time, the Sabah government, together with other plaintiffs, sued Ernst & Young for RM2.4 billion over its audits of Sabah Development Bank, alleging that EY issued unqualified opinions for years even though, according to the claim, 85.94% of the bank’s loan portfolio had been recorded as non-performing loans by FY2018. Both claims remain before the courts, and the allegations have not been tested at trial. The cases will turn on negligence and evidence. But they expose a deeper structural tension that the courts cannot resolve. There is a gap between what an audit opinion actually asserts and what investors assume it guarantees. The lawsuits concern alleged audit failures. The broader issue, however, exists even where there is no allegation of failure. To see that tension clearly, it helps to separate alleged audit failure from the routine judgements in every set of audited accounts. Serba Dinamik and Sabah Development Bank are outlier cases. The structural issue is visible in ordinary audits of Malaysia’s largest companies, whose auditors have not been accused of anything. Maybank’s FY2025 audited accounts provide one illustration. The auditors identified expected credit losses on loans, advances and financing as a Key Audit Matter (KAM). These assets represent 64.3% of the group’s total assets. The auditors stated that measuring expected credit losses (ECL) “requires the application of significant judgement and increased complexity”, involving forward looking factors, probability weighted scenarios and management overlays. They tested models, challenged assumptions and engaged credit modelling specialists. They found no material exceptions. The opinion was unqualified. Tenaga Nasional Bhd’s FY2025 statements offer another. Post employment benefit liabilities of RM13.3 billion at group level were valued using actuarial assumptions on salary increases, medical cost inflation and discount rates. The auditors “focused on this area because of the significant estimates made by management”, checked assumptions against historical data and compared discount rates to market yields with valuation experts. They found no material exceptions. The opinion was unqualified. These are not presented as cases of audit failure. The system is working as designed. Yet TNB reports that a one percentage point movement in the discount rate can change its defined benefit obligation by more than RM1 billion. Maybank’s KAM similarly describes extensive audit procedures without showing investors the range of possible outcomes. The KAM explains the judgement, but not how sensitive the number may be. International Standard on Auditing (ISA) 701 requires auditors to communicate KAMs and allow them to highlight matters requiring significant auditor attention, while the opinion remains on the financial statements as a whole. But the framework is binary while uncertainty is not. Two competent valuers may reach different estimates, and a figure can be reasonable without being the only supportable answer. KAMs can therefore become lists of procedures rather than explanations of risk. Estimation uncertainty exists on a continuum while audit reporting remains categorical. The question is not whether KAMs should exist, but whether they tell investors enough about how uncertain the most consequential numbers really are. Malaysia’s Audit Oversight Board has identified “failure to sufficiently review significant risk areas and significant judgements” as a recurring enforcement concern. The International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) highlighted in its November 2025 statement the importance of high-quality valuation practices, appropriate use of valuation experts and rigorous audit assessment. The International Forum of Independent Audit Regulators (IFIAR) has likewise identified accounting estimates, including fair value measurement, as an area where audit regulators have consistently found deficiencies. When auditors use KAMs to flag a valuation without qualifying the opinion, they are telling investors that the matter involved significant judgement but that the financial statements nevertheless met the requirements for an unmodified opinion. That may be technically correct for Maybank and TNB. But the Serba Dinamik case illustrates how insufficient that signal can be for investors. The concern is not simply whether auditors get the judgement wrong. Even a sound audit can leave investors unable to see how fragile a reasonable estimate may be. That is the gap the current reporting model should address. Four reforms would help. First, require sensitivity disclosure in the KAM. Auditors should disclose the reasonable range of outcomes and its impact on the financial statements. TNB’s statements already include sensitivity analysis on discount rate assumptions. This information should be connected directly to the KAM, rather than leaving investors to piece the implications together from different sections of the annual report. Second, consider graduated reporting for significant estimation uncertainty. Such reporting could signal that an estimate falls within an acceptable range but remains highly sensitive, without implying that there is a material misstatement. The existing Emphasis of Matter framework under ISA 706 could provide a starting point. Third, require independent valuation review for specified material Level 3 assets. A second valuation would provide an additional check on management bias. The auditor could assess the divergence as evidence and consider the additional data point when applying professional scepticism. Fourth, strengthen audit committee disclosure. Audit committees should disclose how they challenged management’s fair value assumptions. If the committee accepted management’s numbers without meaningful scrutiny, that should be visible to shareholders. None of these solutions are radical. Each builds on existing frameworks, including Malaysian Financial Reporting Standard 13 (MFRS 13), ISA 701, ISA 540 and Malaysia’s corporate governance code. They require recognition that the current approach to fair value auditing, while technically sound, is insufficiently transparent for the risks involved. Judgement is unavoidable. Opacity is not. A KAM should do more than say, “we looked at this”. It should help investors understand what drove the estimate, how sensitive it is and what could change the auditor’s assessment. A “clean” audit opinion was never meant to guarantee that every number is right. But as financial statements rely increasingly on complex estimates, audit reporting should show more clearly how uncertain the most consequential numbers are. Hijat A Jabbar and Siti Zabedah Saidin are professors of accounting at Universiti Utara Malaysia. The content is a snapshot from Publisher. Refer to the original content for accurate info. Maybank’s KAM similarly describes extensive audit procedures without showing investors the range of possible outcomes. The KAM explains the judgement, but not how sensitive the number may be. International Standard on Auditing (ISA) 701 requires auditors to communicate KAMs and allow them to highlight matters requiring significant auditor attention, while the opinion remains on the financial statements as a whole. But the framework is binary while uncertainty is not. Two competent valuers may reach different estimates, and a figure can be reasonable without being the only supportable answer. KAMs can therefore become lists of procedures rather than explanations of risk. Estimation uncertainty exists on a continuum while audit reporting remains categorical. The question is not whether KAMs should exist, but whether they tell investors enough about how uncertain the most consequential numbers really are. Malaysia’s Audit Oversight Board has identified “failure to sufficiently review significant risk areas and significant judgements” as a recurring enforcement concern. The International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) highlighted in its November 2025 statement the importance of high-quality valuation practices, appropriate use of valuation experts and rigorous audit assessment. The International Forum of Independent Audit Regulators (IFIAR) has likewise identified accounting estimates, including fair value measurement, as an area where audit regulators have consistently found deficiencies. When auditors use KAMs to flag a valuation without qualifying the opinion, they are telling investors that the matter involved significant judgement but that the financial statements nevertheless met the requirements for an unmodified opinion. That may be technically correct for Maybank and TNB. But the Serba Dinamik case illustrates how insufficient that signal can be for investors. The concern is not simply whether auditors get the judgement wrong. Even a sound audit can leave investors unable to see how fragile a reasonable estimate may be. That is the gap the current reporting model should address. Four reforms would help. First, require sensitivity disclosure in the KAM. Auditors should disclose the reasonable range of outcomes and its impact on the financial statements. TNB’s statements already include sensitivity analysis on discount rate assumptions. This information should be connected directly to the KAM, rather than leaving investors to piece the implications together from different sections of the annual report. Second, consider graduated reporting for significant estimation uncertainty. Such reporting could signal that an estimate falls within an acceptable range but remains highly sensitive, without implying that there is a material misstatement. The existing Emphasis of Matter framework under ISA 706 could provide a starting point. Third, require independent valuation review for specified material Level 3 assets. A second valuation would provide an additional check on management bias. The auditor could assess the divergence as evidence and consider the additional data point when applying professional scepticism. Fourth, strengthen audit committee disclosure. Audit committees should disclose how they challenged management’s fair value assumptions. If the committee accepted management’s numbers without meaningful scrutiny, that should be visible to shareholders. None of these solutions are radical. Each builds on existing frameworks, including Malaysian Financial Reporting Standard 13 (MFRS 13), ISA 701, ISA 540 and Malaysia’s corporate governance code. They require recognition that the current approach to fair value auditing, while technically sound, is insufficiently transparent for the risks involved. Judgement is unavoidable. Opacity is not. A KAM should do more than say, “we looked at this”. It should help investors understand what drove the estimate, how sensitive it is and what could change the auditor’s assessment. A “clean” audit opinion was never meant to guarantee that every number is right. But as financial statements rely increasingly on complex estimates, audit reporting should show more clearly how uncertain the most consequential numbers are. title: 'Budget 2027 may bring SST exemptions, income tax relief for middle-income earners — CIMB Securities
body:
'

KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 18): Budget 2027 could see further sales and service tax (SST) exemptions to reduce costs embedded in businesses, alongside possible personal income tax relief for middle-income taxpayers, according to CIMB Securities.

CIMB Securities said there is scope for the government to broaden SST exemptions for production-related inputs, as businesses continue to face elevated energy, logistics and other operating costs.

It expects further SST relief to reduce government collections by about RM1 billion, although underlying growth should still lift SST revenue by 5.5% to RM72 billion in 2027.

Unlike the goods and services tax (GST), the SST does not have a general input tax credit mechanism, meaning businesses may pay tax on inputs without being able to deduct it against tax charged on their own sales. This can result in tax costs being embedded through the supply chain, CIMB noted.

CIMB said in a note extending selected exemptions is likely to be the more immediate option in Budget 2027, while a broader input tax credit mechanism could be introduced from 2028 or later because of the additional administrative and refund framework required.

At the same time, CIMB sees room for targeted personal income tax relief for middle-income taxpayers, particularly households facing higher living costs but receiving less direct cash assistance.

As an illustration, the research house said tax rates for chargeable income of RM50,001 to RM70,000 and RM70,001 to RM100,000 could each be reduced by one percentage point to 10% and 18% respectively.

The current 25% tax bracket could also be split, with a 24% rate applied to chargeable income between RM100,001 and RM150,000.

Such a package could provide annual tax savings of RM200 for those with RM70,000 in chargeable income, RM500 at RM100,000 and as much as RM1,000 for those earning RM150,000 and above, CIMB estimated.

It said the illustrative package would cost the government about RM800 million annually.

More broadly, CIMB expects Budget 2027 to continue providing household support while maintaining fiscal consolidation, forecasting the fiscal deficit to narrow slightly to 3.4% of gross domestic product in 2027 from an estimated 3.5% in 2026.

The research house also expects cash assistance under Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah to increase by RM2 billion to RM17 billion, supported partly by lower fuel subsidy spending.

CIMB forecasts petrol and diesel subsidies to fall to RM32 billion in 2027 from RM41 billion, creating room for higher household assistance and development spending while keeping the government on its fiscal consolidation path.

Budget 2027, the fifth Madani Budget and the second under the 13th Malaysia Plan, is scheduled to be tabled in Parliament on Oct 9. The Ministry of Finance has said the budget will focus on areas including cost-of-living pressures, business competitiveness and productivity, while maintaining fiscal discipline.

title: 'HLB Targets Wealthy Clients With New opus Privilege Ecosystem
body:
'

Hong Leong Bank is strengthening its affluent banking strategy with HLB opus, an invitation-only payment and lifestyle programme built for selected high-value clients.

The launch combines premium banking, travel benefits and wealth relationships into a single proposition.


At the centre is Southeast Asia’s first ceramic credit card.

HLB opus is also the first payment experience in Malaysia to use the Visa Infinite Privilege tier.

However, the bigger story is not the card material.

HLB is using opus to connect business banking, private wealth management and premium lifestyle benefits under one customer relationship.

HLB Connects Business Success With Personal Wealth

HLB calls the strategy its “One Bank” client success model.

The approach reflects how many high-net-worth customers interact with banks.

Their financial relationships can span business financing, corporate accounts, investments, private banking and personal spending.

HLB wants opus to sit at the personal end of that journey.

Business & Corporate Banking supports entrepreneurship and company growth.

Private Banking helps clients structure and preserve wealth.

Personal Financial Services then translates that relationship into travel, lifestyle and rewards benefits.

The model allows HLB to position opus as a product earned through a broader financial relationship rather than a conventional premium credit card application.

Ceramic Card Reinforces Exclusivity

The physical HLB opus card uses Convego Ceramic technology from Giesecke+Devrient.

Ceramic remains uncommon in the payment card industry, where most premium offerings rely on metal.

The HLB card is manufactured using extreme heat and pressure before undergoing diamond finishing.

The result is designed to be scratch resistant while offering a smooth texture and reflective appearance.

HLB sees the material as part of the product’s wider symbolism.

The name “opus” comes from the Latin word associated with work or achievement.

That concept is intended to connect the physical card with the professional and financial achievements of the clients invited to hold it.

Andrew Jong, HLB Managing Director of Personal Financial Services, said the product recognises the personal stories, sacrifices and ambitions behind client success.

Visa Infinite Privilege Expands Global Access

The privileges attached to the card extend well beyond payments.

HLB opus uses Visa Infinite Privilege, one of Visa’s highest-tier premium offerings.

Clients receive unlimited access to Plaza Premium Lounges around the world.

The package also includes immigration fast-track passes and access to selected Visa private clubs.

Additional status-matching benefits include Harrods Gold, ALL Accor+ Explorer Gold and Banyan Voyager.

These benefits target customers who travel frequently for business and leisure.

Visa Malaysia said affluent consumers are increasingly looking for experiences that feel personal and differentiated.

That shift is pushing premium banking products away from simple cashback and points propositions.

Enrich Partnership Strengthens Travel Rewards

Malaysia Airlines’ Enrich programme plays another important role in the HLB opus ecosystem.

Clients receive 60,000 Enrich Points after payment of the annual fee.

HLB has also created a higher conversion tier designed to reward overseas spending.

The bank says the arrangement gives opus clients the strongest Enrich Points earning potential in the region.

Cardholders can additionally earn one Elite Point for every RM10,000 spent overseas.

Elite Points can help travellers progress through Enrich status tiers.

The partnership also connects customers to reward opportunities across Malaysia Airlines and other carriers in the oneworld alliance.

Malaysia Aviation Group said the collaboration is intended to extend premium service beyond individual flights and into the wider travel experience.

HLB Looks Beyond Traditional Luxury Banking

The introduction of opus reflects changing expectations among affluent banking customers.

Luxury financial products once competed mainly through card materials, airport lounges and concierge services.

Those benefits still matter.

However, wealthy customers increasingly expect banks to understand their wider business, investment and personal needs.

HLB appears to be responding by combining multiple banking divisions around the same client.

That can create deeper relationships and make it harder for competitors to win individual parts of a customer’s financial business.

For HLB, the value of opus may therefore extend far beyond spending on the card itself.

Wealth Management Remains a Key Growth Area

HLB has been expanding its wealth capabilities alongside its business and corporate banking operations.

The bank’s Private Bank works with international wealth partners including Lombard Odier.

That gives HLB access to broader investment and wealth-management expertise for high-net-worth clients.

HLB opus adds a lifestyle layer on top of those capabilities.

The strategy allows the bank to follow a client from business growth through wealth accumulation and eventually into legacy planning.

Premium travel and lifestyle services then become part of that broader relationship.

HLB opus Is Really About Client Retention

The ceramic card may attract attention, but HLB’s larger objective is relationship depth.

An invite-only product gives the bank another way to recognise and retain its highest-value customers.

Premium rewards can strengthen loyalty among clients who already use HLB for corporate, private or personal banking.

At the same time, the exclusivity of the product can reinforce the perceived value of the wider banking relationship.

That makes HLB opus as much a customer strategy as a credit card launch.

Its combination of ceramic design, Visa Infinite Privilege services and Malaysia Airlines rewards gives HLB a distinctive premium proposition.

More importantly, it gives the bank another tool for keeping business, wealth and lifestyle banking under one roof.

title: 'Axis REIT ‘well positioned’ against rate risks amid RM250 mil deal pipeline — analyst
body: 'Axis REIT ‘well positioned’ against rate risks amid RM250 mil deal pipeline — analyst KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Longer-term financing secured much earlier is now providing Axis REIT (KL:AXREIT) cushion against rising interest rates as the real estate investment trust pursues deals, an analyst said. A 25-basis-point increase in policy rate would potentially raise its cost of borrowings by just 0.1 percentage-point to 4.06%, Maybank Investment Bank said, noting that Axis REIT has locked in 10-year and seven-year financing facilities over the past 12 months when rates were more favourable. “With the completion of signed acquisitions, gearing is expected to rise to around 39%, still having ample headroom before any equity raising is required,” the research house said. Axis REIT owns and manages more than 70 office and industrial assets worth over RM5 billion in Klang Valley, Penang, Johor, Pahang, Negeri Sembilan and Kedah. The trust is in the midst of acquiring a distribution centre, a warehouse, and an industrial complex for RM193 million combined. The stated aim is to nearly double the asset under management to RM10 billion by 2030, driven by high-growth sectors and key industrial hubs throughout Peninsular Malaysia. In the near term, Axis REIT has a RM250 million acquisition pipeline currently under negotiation, of which one or two transactions could be announced before year-end, Maybank Investment said and maintained its “buy” call on the trust. “We believe its acquisition pipeline should provide further income visibility” with most ongoing transactions fully occupied and carrying weighted average lease expiry of five years or longer, the research house said. Axis REIT has rebounded from its September lows when the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years, sending global bond yields higher and triggering concerns of rising borrowing costs. Still, 10 out of 12 research houses tracked by Bloomberg recommend investors to “buy” Axis REIT and two are on “hold” calls. The average target price is RM2.22, a potential gain of up to 21% in the next 12 months from current price of RM1.84. The content is a snapshot from Publisher. title: 'DNB secures RM5.2 bil for next phase of 5G growth, MOF retains special share
body: 'Digital Nasional Berhad (DNB) has completed a RM5.2 billion financing exercise as it moves into the next phase of Malaysia’s 5G development.  The financing comes as the nation’s first 5G network has secured a new long-term spectrum assignment, while the government (via MOF Inc) will exit as an ordinary shareholder.  CelcomDigi, Maxis and YTL are expected to hold equal ownership in DNB. Transition is expected to be completed in early Q4 2026, however, MOF Inc. will retain a special share.  DNB completes RM5.2 billion financing  DNB said it has completed a RM5.2 billion Syndicated Islamic Term Financing exercise, which it described as among the largest syndicated loan facilities ever arranged for an unlisted company in Malaysia.  Maybank Investment Bank acted as Mandated Lead Arranger, Bookrunner and Coordinating Arranger, while AmInvestment Bank, CIMB Islamic Bank, RHB Islamic Bank and United Overseas Bank Malaysia were Joint Mandated Lead Arrangers. AmInvestment Bank also acted as financial adviser to DNB.  The financing will also be used to refinance DNB’s Government Guarantee Revolving Credit Facility (GGRCF), which expired on 29 September 2026.  According to DNB, the new financing provides a sustainable long-term funding structure to support its future growth.  The financing is also expected to reduce the need for additional equity funding from DNB’s mobile network operator shareholders, based on DNB’s current regulatory commitments and funding requirements.  DNB CEO Datuk Azman Ismail said, “The successful completion of this RM5.2 billion financing exercise marks a significant milestone for DNB and reflects strong confidence in our business fundamentals, operational track record and long-term role in Malaysia’s digital economy. This financing provides DNB with a sustainable platform to operate on its own, continue investing in network enhancement and capacity expansion, and leverage our expanded spectrum assets.”  He added, “As Malaysia progresses under the dual network framework, DNB remains committed to providing world-class digital infrastructure that supports our shareholders, customers, enterprises and government agencies. With strong financing, enhanced spectrum resources and a proven nationwide 5G platform, DNB is well positioned to support the Government’s AI Nation aspirations and help power Malaysia’s next phase of digital growth.”  DNB gets 15-year 5G spectrum certainty  DNB has also received the full 100MHz block in the 3.3GHz to 3.4GHz band, known as F0, while its entire 240MHz spectrum holding has been converted from Apparatus Assignment (AA) into Spectrum Assignment (SA).  The Spectrum Assignment for a 15-year period awarded by the MCMC provides greater long-term certainty over spectrum availability and it takes effect from 1 October 2026.  By securing 200MHz of the contiguous mid-band spectrum (3.3 to 3.5GHz), DNB has a stronger foundation to modernise the network, expand indoor building solutions, enhance coverage and maximise spectrum utilisation. In addition, DNB also has 2x 20Hz blocks of the low band spectrum with 703MHz to 723MHz and 758Hz to 778MHz.  DNB said its spectrum holdings will also support higher network capacity and efficiency, as well as technologies including Massive MIMO, carrier aggregation, 5G Advanced and AI-driven network capabilities.  MOF to retain special share in DNB  While the recent financing facilitates MOF Inc.’s planned exit as an ordinary shareholder of DNB, the government via MOF Inc will continue to retain a special share in the company. According to DNB, the special share will safeguard national interests and ensure continued stewardship over key strategic matters.  Following the share transfer, the mobile network operator shareholders would assume a greater role in jointly steering DNB’s strategic and operational priorities.  In a separate statement issued by CelcomDigi, the telco says it will bring its scale, nationwide network assets and more than 30 years of telecommunications experience to support DNB. This includes leveraging on existing infrastructure, sites and capabilities to drive cost efficiencies, support coverage expansion and accelerate indoor 5G deployment.

title: 'MH WellFest Cambodia 2026 Strengthens ASEAN Healthcare Cooperation
body: 'MH WellFest Cambodia 2026 is a healthcare cooperation between Cambodia and Malaysia, merging medicine with financial services and community health in Phnom Penh. The event was held on October 3 and 4 at Borey Peng Huoth Eco Park and was organized by Maybank Cambodia and the Malaysia Healthcare Travel Council. The move is part of a wider trend in ASEAN to make cross-border healthcare more accessible. The event showcased practical means of streamlining medical travel in the region by connecting Cambodian families with Malaysian healthcare providers and financial services. Malaysian Healthcare Expertise Reaches Cambodia The event gathered 14 leading Malaysian hospital groups and medical specialists in Phnom Penh. Cambodian families were able to have discussions with health professionals about preventive health care, specialty care and potential medical travel arrangements. This direct engagement can help patients to better understand treatment options before traveling overseas. It also builds linkages between the healthcare providers of both countries and raises greater awareness in the region of Malaysia’s medical services. Maybank Connects Healthcare With Financial Services Maybank Cambodia took the opportunity to showcase cross border payment solutions, medical travel privileges and financial planning support at the event. These services are intended to help families overcome some of the financial and administrative barriers to arranging treatment overseas. The addition of banking support with access to healthcare provides a more rounded medical travel experience. For patients considering treatment in Malaysia, planning for finances can be an important part of managing the transportation, hospital expenses and other associated costs. Community Wellness Takes Center Stage MH WellFest wasn’t just about medical travel, it was about preventive health and community participation. The MH WellFest Run added a public wellness aspect to the event with over 800 runners and walkers in the 5km and 10km categories. Visitors also could attend health screening booths, medical presentations and family-oriented cultural activities. Malaysia has been marketing itself as a regional hub for international patients looking for specialized medical services. title: 'Stock Focus
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 1): CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL: CIMB) could potentially raise its RM2 billion capital return commitment to increase the chances of its share buyback programme garnering investor acceptance, according to MBSB Research.  A higher capital-return commitment could help offset potential disappointment among investors who are expecting a larger portion of the RM2 billion to be returned via special dividends, the research house said.  “To increase its chances of success, we think there is a likelihood of CIMB positively revising to the RM2.0 billion figure, and that CIMB is confident enough on its ability to garner sufficient capital before signalling to the market via share buybacks,” MBSB Research said in a note on Thursday.  “We would not put it past CIMB’s management to pull off such a manoeuvre — they’ve surprised us positively multiple times in the past,” it added.  MBSB Research noted that share buybacks have historically not been successful in Malaysia. CIMB’s share buybacks make up a portion of its RM2 billion capital return scheme, of which RM700 million has already been returned via special dividends.  The primary purpose of the share buybacks is for CIMB to further drive its earnings per share, return on equity (ROE) and dividend per share figures, MBSB Research noted, particularly as the bank is slightly behind on its ROE target for the financial year ending Dec 31, 2026 (FY2026).  The research house noted CIMB has been buying back shares every day, tallying up to 20.76 million shares for RM163 million since Sept 21 thus far.  Who could follow CIMB?  CIMB’s share buyback programme is also being watched for its potential implications on other banks, according to MBSB Research.  The research house described the programme as the first major share buyback scheme by a Malaysian bank for capital management purposes in many years, and said a successful outcome could encourage other large banks to consider similar measures.  It listed Public Bank Bhd (KL: PBBANK) and RHB Bank Bhd (KL: RHBBANK) as possible candidates.  Public Bank, it noted, has already received shareholder approval for a share buyback of up to 10% of its shares, although it has not done any yet. Its management has maintained that this is a capital optimisation option rather than a set path they want to go down, the research house added.  RHB Bank, meanwhile, has high capital ratios and historically releases excess capital via larger payouts in the fourth quarter, MBSB Research noted. It is currently preparing a new capital release plan, which is scheduled to be announced by the first quarter of FY2027, the research house added.  MBSB Research maintained its “buy” call on CIMB but with a lower target price of RM9.20 from RM9.29, based on an unchanged FY2027 forecast price-to-book value of 1.33 times.  At the time of writing, shares of CIMB were down three sen or 0.39% at RM7.76, valuing the lender at RM84 billion.

title: 'MACC Remands Corporate Brothers in RM10m Investment Probe, Seizes 15 Luxury Cars Among Others
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 1): Two corporate figures, who are brothers, are being remanded for five days over an alleged abuse of position involving an investment of about RM10 million. The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) obtained the remand order, effective from Thursday until next Monday (Oct 5), from Magistrate Ezrene Zakariah at the Putrajaya Magistrate’s Court on Thursday morning. According to a source, the two men, in their 40s and 50s and carrying the titles of Datuk Seri and Datuk Wira respectively, were detained at about 9pm on Wednesday after giving their statements at the MACC headquarters here. Initial investigations found that the duo were suspected of acting in collusion in the alleged offence in late 2020. “They are also believed to have colluded with an officer of an education-based foundation to approve an investment of about RM10 million in an investment company owned by the elder brother,” the source told Bernama. The MACC also seized 15 luxury cars, 12 high-powered motorcycles, five luxury watches, three bracelets and about RM30,000 in cash. MACC chief commissioner Datuk Seri Abd Halim Aman confirmed the matter when contacted and said the case is being investigated under Section 23 of the MACC Act 2009. title: 'Rapidus Taps Four Malaysian Firms as Design Solution Associates for CORE Ecosystem
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 6): Rapidus Corporation has roped in Malaysian firms — GreatAsic Technology Sdn Bhd, Infinecs Systems Sdn Bhd, Oppstar Bhd's (KL:OPPSTAR) Oppstar Technology Sdn Bhd and SkyeChip Bhd (KL:SKYECHIP) — as design solution associates to support the development of its global chip ecosystem framework. The Japan-backed Rapidus said it will establish the Rapidus Collaborative Open Rapid Ecosystem (CORE), a global ecosystem framework to support the development and mass production of cutting-edge semiconductors. As the first Rapidus CORE initiative, Rapidus said it is forming a group of design solution associates, which include 17 firms. "Today, semiconductor development requires more than just manufacturing technology; it is essential to integrate the entire semiconductor value chain — including research institutions, EDA (Electronic Design Automation), IP (intellectual property), design and manufacturing — to provide customers with a development and production infrastructure they can rely on. "Further, amid a global shortage of cutting-edge semiconductor talent, it is crucial to build a design ecosystem that enables customers to begin development at an early stage by collaborating with design-related companies," Rapidus said in a statement on Monday. The 17 firms include Malaysian companies, namely GreatAsic Technology, Infinecs Systems, Oppstar Technology, and SkyeChip. Other firms include Japan's Dai Nippon Printing, TOPPAN Inc, Toshiba Information Systems, MavissDesign, and NSW Inc and London-based AION Silicon. Also listed were Indian firms namely HCL Technologies Ltd, Infosys Ltd, Moschip Technologies ltd, and Wipro Ltd; US-based companies Cadence Design Systems and Synopsys, as well as Singapore's Quest Global Services. Design solution associates will serve as a bridge between customers and Rapidus, providing each company's design resources and specialised expertise to support the rapid evolution of semiconductor development. This will enable Rapidus to strengthen its support system — from design through manufacturing — to meet customer needs both in Japan and overseas. Moving forward, Rapidus will expand its CORE offerings beyond design to include EDA, IP and other categories. Rapidus is a Japanese state-backed semiconductor company founded in 2022 to mass-produce cutting-edge two-nanometer logic chips domestically by 2027. It was established through a partnership between the Japanese government and major private corporations, including Toyota, Sony, NTT, and SoftBank, to reduce Japan's reliance on foreign chipmakers like TSMC. title: 'DNB secures RM5.2 bil for next phase of 5G growth, MOF retains special share
body: 'Digital Nasional Berhad (DNB) has completed a RM5.2 billion financing exercise as it moves into the next phase of Malaysia’s 5G development. The financing comes as the nation’s first 5G network has secured a new long-term spectrum assignment, while the government (via MOF Inc) will exit as an ordinary shareholder. CelcomDigi, Maxis and YTL are expected to hold equal ownership in DNB. Transition is expected to be completed in early Q4 2026, however, MOF Inc. will retain a special share. DNB completes RM5.2 billion financing DNB said it has completed a RM5.2 billion Syndicated Islamic Term Financing exercise, which it described as among the largest syndicated loan facilities ever arranged for an unlisted company in Malaysia. Maybank Investment Bank acted as Mandated Lead Arranger, Bookrunner and Coordinating Arranger, while AmInvestment Bank, CIMB Islamic Bank, RHB Islamic Bank and United Overseas Bank Malaysia were Joint Mandated Lead Arrangers. AmInvestment Bank also acted as financial adviser to DNB. The financing will also be used to refinance DNB’s Government Guarantee Revolving Credit Facility (GGRCF), which expired on 29 September 2026. According to DNB, the new financing provides a sustainable long-term funding structure to support its future growth. The financing is also expected to reduce the need for additional equity funding from DNB’s mobile network operator shareholders, based on DNB’s current regulatory commitments and funding requirements. DNB CEO Datuk Azman Ismail said, “The successful completion of this RM5.2 billion financing exercise marks a significant milestone for DNB and reflects strong confidence in our business fundamentals, operational track record and long-term role in Malaysia’s digital economy. This financing provides DNB with a sustainable platform to operate on its own, continue investing in network enhancement and capacity expansion, and leverage our expanded spectrum assets.” He added, “As Malaysia progresses under the dual network framework, DNB remains committed to providing world-class digital infrastructure that supports our shareholders, customers, enterprises and government agencies. With strong financing, enhanced spectrum resources and a proven nationwide 5G platform, DNB is well positioned to support the Government’s AI Nation aspirations and help power Malaysia’s next phase of digital growth.” DNB gets 15-year 5G spectrum certainty DNB has also received the full 100MHz block in the 3.3GHz to 3.4GHz band, known as F0, while its entire 240MHz spectrum holding has been converted from Apparatus Assignment (AA) into Spectrum Assignment (SA). The Spectrum Assignment for a 15-year period awarded by the MCMC provides greater long-term certainty over spectrum availability and it takes effect from 1 October 2026. By securing 200MHz of the contiguous mid-band spectrum (3.3 to 3.5GHz), DNB has a stronger foundation to modernise the network, expand indoor building solutions, enhance coverage and maximise spectrum utilisation. In addition, DNB also has 2x 20Hz blocks of the low band spectrum with 703MHz to 723MHz and 758Hz to 778MHz. DNB said its spectrum holdings will also support higher network capacity and efficiency, as well as technologies including Massive MIMO, carrier aggregation, 5G Advanced and AI-driven network capabilities. MOF to retain special share in DNB While the recent financing facilitates MOF Inc.’s planned exit as an ordinary shareholder of DNB, the government via MOF Inc will continue to retain a special share in the company. According to DNB, the special share will safeguard national interests and ensure continued stewardship over key strategic matters. Following the share transfer, the mobile network operator shareholders would assume a greater role in jointly steering DNB’s strategic and operational priorities. In a separate statement issued by CelcomDigi, the telco says it will bring its scale, nationwide network assets and more than 30 years of telecommunications experience to support DNB. This includes leveraging on existing infrastructure, sites and capabilities to drive cost efficiencies, support coverage expansion and accelerate indoor 5G deployment.
